utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court is in session. Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court) (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody, to the interpreters. Does everybody hear me? The Prosecution, the Defence, does the accused hear me? Very well. We can resume. We had reached the cross-examination of Major Whitworth. Please have the witness brought in. I can see that Mr. Kehoe is standing: I thought the Defence was supposed to be standing up, not you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is. All due respect to my colleague across the chamber, but I neglected, prior to adjourning yesterday evening, to move to admit the various exhibits that we spoke about and if I could just take care of that housekeeping chore at this juncture, I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There were many. Does the Defence have any comments to make about these? Mr. Hayman, do you have anything that you would like to say about the many exhibits that were presented as evidence, during the testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Only two, Mr. President. We have no objection except for two, and one is the -- I believe it's the videotape which depicts fighting and Darko Kraljevic running across a lawn firing, I think, from both hands. There was no date for this tape, and if it's offered simply as a photograph of Darko Kraljevic, I have no objection. But I would ask, without a date, that it be admitted for that limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it is admitted not only for identification purposes, but also to admit it for the fact that Darko Kraljevic is, in fact, fighting on behalf of the HVO. We do not have the date for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you yourself were suggesting that we take a still. You said you wanted a still. What was interesting to you was that there was a particular sequence, and you said that we could even make a still of something here. Wouldn't that be enough or do you want the entire video to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I would like the entire video to be admitted, Mr. President. With regard, there were many stills taken, some at the request of Defence, and certainly the Prosecutor has no objection to any still taken of any video that the Prosecutor moves into evidence. Nevertheless, I think the entire video is instructive on several different levels for the Chamber. When the BBC gave us that particular piece of video, we did not have a date for that video. I wish we did. I simply don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you want this to be moved into evidence, couldn't you ask the BBC to identify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will go become to the BBC and ask them to go through their archives and attempt to give a more certain date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will just hold that particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you maintain your objection? We will ask for the date to be found out, but does that now satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand counsel to be offering to try again and find the date and I suggest we hold him in abeyance and see if the BBC can come through. My only other objection, Mr. President, is to 447 which are photographs of Grbavica purportedly from 1997, and our objection there is one of relevance. 1997 is two years after the indictment in this case, and some four years after or three and a half years after the end of the time period of the allegations. So we have a relevance objection to 447.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can't sustain that objection because the Judges are the ones who decide on relevance. All right, so we are going to take the exhibit. Mr. Hayman, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I need a witness to proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that does seem to be important. You just had to ask it and there you have it. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, you are now going to be asked questions by the accused's Defence counsel, the accused who is in this room. Did you have a restful evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, sir, yes, despite the weather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The weather, that we can't do anything about it and you can't either. Mr. Hayman, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Whitworth. My name is Russell Hayman and together with my colleague Anto Nobilo, I represent General Blaskic in these proceedings. You arrived in Central Bosnia in May of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you took over the liaison officer position sometime later in June of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, it was the last week of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, when you are asked the questions, look at the counsel, but when you answer, please answer facing the Judges. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your statement of the 14th of May 1997, paragraph 2, you indicated you were introduced as the Vitez liaison officer at the beginning of June 1993. Is that no longer your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Would it be possible for me to have a copy of my statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection to that. If the court permits it, I would welcome it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the request of the witness, there is a statement -- copy of his statement that counsel is referring to, and I just was providing it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would direct your attention to page 2, paragraph 2, the top line.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In reply to your question, this was a statement taken, I think, nearly two years ago, and the circumstances under which I made the statement were quite difficult for me in that it was sometime since I had been in Bosnia. I had nothing to do with the armed forces at all and had made every effort to put my memories of my experiences there, to the back of my mind. And it's since I've been called to the court that I've actually taken the time to recall these things, look at the photographs that I've had, and do a bit of background that's helped me fill in some of the details. So I think there are probably one or two things in here that are not quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So your testimony is your memory today is better than it was in May of 1997 when you gave this statement because you've had the opportunity to study some documents and refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I have had the opportunity to look at the MILINFOSUMs which I filled in personally at the end of each day with the intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have looked at, and I take it, all the Prince of Wales own unredacted MILINFOSUMs?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A fair number of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Anything else that you've used to help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Just the extensive collection of photographs that I took at the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What in those MILINFOSUMs indicates that you took over your liaison officer position in May and not in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm specifically referred to in the MILINFOSUMs as the Vitez LO, but in about the 25th or 26th of May. That position had not existed up until that time, and as such was referred to from there on in for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, did you receive a briefing prior to taking over your position from your predecessor Mr. Hay?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did indeed so, yes, it was a brief one which involved, really, a tour around the area and an introduction to a few of the senior people, both Muslims and Croats, army representatives and HVO representatives of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hay tell you whether he had had a meeting with Colonel Blaskic earlier in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He intimated at the time, if I recall, that that was, in fact, the case, that he had had a meeting. He had actually met Colonel Blaskic prior to my meeting Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll pause briefly after your answers to allow the interpretation to be completed. Did he tell you anything about that meeting or conversation?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you do not have any notes or diaries or calendars of your service in Bosnia that you can use to further refresh your recollection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct. At the time, I did keep a detailed notebook, but that was -- and that's what I used to return the information that I had at the end of each day which became part of the MILINFOSUMs, but those notebooks were handed in at the end of my operational tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Handed in to whom?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Handed in to the MILINFO people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The British battalion?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke to the court yesterday of meeting Colonel Blaskic in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many meetings did you have with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In total, maybe a dozen throughout the entire period, the majority of which I'd organised on behalf of Colonel Alastair, but most of the meetings were with the absence of Colonel Blaskic and were with his liaison officer, Darko Gelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the specific discussions or content of any of those 12 meetings?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: One particular occasion, Colonel Blaskic was concerned about the Nova Bila hospital evacuations. That was a meeting between he and Colonel Alastair.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was he concerned about?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The number of casualties in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had there been a request to evacuate critically wounded from Nova Bila to more adequate medical facilities outside of the Vitez enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was a repeated request that we had had from the hospital on numerous occasions prior to Colonel Blaskic's request to Colonel Alastair, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there a party that objected or delayed, in some way, those evacuations?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. Whenever a request was made, we passed that request on behalf of the HVO to Kiseljak because, of course, we were bound by their direction as to whether we could or could not evacuate those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What concern did Colonel Blaskic express about a pending evacuation, then, at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My recollection is vague, but I would have assumed it would be about the number of casualties and the ability of the limited medical facilities to deal with the number of those casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, weren't there significant delays in the ability of the HVO to evacuate their critically wounded from Nova Bila due to conditions and restrictions imposed on those evacuations by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think there was a time on, one or two occasions, from my recollection, where we looked on behalf of 3 corps representatives to allow movement of any vehicles including those from Nova Bila hospital, because the accusation was that we were evacuating soldiers in amongst those casualties, regardless if those soldiers were injured themselves. Hence we went through quite a promulgated and complicated triage system involving myself and several U.N. medical officers to determine whether people being evacuated from Nova Bila when they actually happened, the evacuations occurred, were actually medically in need of evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for scouring your memory on that point. We will return to the Nova Bila facility, but for now do you recall the specific content of any other discussions which you personally participated in with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not at the moment, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said in your testimony on direct that Colonel Blaskic was informed about far away places like Vares. Can you give us any examples in what ways he was informed about distant locales?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We would or I would be given information via Colonel Blaskic's liaison officer, Darko Gelic, about incidents and military activity in areas outside the Lasva Valley. It was particularly common that we would get -- I can't remember the name of the place, but somewhere north-east of the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In terms of Colonel Blaskic's own ability to go and inspect these other parts of his operational zone and area of responsibility; if Colonel Blaskic, during your tour, wanted to head to the west to inspect, how far could he go without UNPROFOR's security and assistance? How far could Colonel Blaskic travel to the west from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He could go as far as the Travnik T-junction, then head south towards the Prozor, Gornji Vakuf area. The Croat pocket was actually quite small and went as far east as Busovaca, but our impression was that he was regularly moving in and out of the area using the regular helicopter flights that occurred in and out of the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We will return to the subject of helicopters later this morning. But for now, my question was how far to the west could he go, and I take it he could go as far as the T-junction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse, Mr. President, that's not what the witness said. The witness (sic) said how far could he travel in the west and the witness said he could travel down to Prozor and Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is sustained. The witness already answered the question, Mr. Hayman. Move to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The record should reflect I was interrupted in the middle of my question and the objection was on the grounds that I was misstating the testimony which I had not finished stating. I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, if Colonel Blaskic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, continue. We're just talking about the Croatian pocket and the ability of the accused to move around in that area. You were given an answer about that, unless you really are asking a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How far could Colonel Blaskic travel to the north from the Hotel Vitez without UNPROFOR security?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was actually quite limited. The BiH frontlines were quite far south from Zenica and literally around --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: A kilometre?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, maybe a kilometre north from that location, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How far to the east of the Hotel Vitez could Colonel Blaskic travel on the ground without UNPROFOR security and assistance?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Busovaca, the Busovaca on the way to Kiseljak road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lastly, if my compass serves me well, how far could Colonel Blaskic travel to the south from the hotel Vitez without UNPROFOR security and assistance?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Three or four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Through Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, it could get further up towards Zacilja which is where the original HVO territory was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But going around through Gacice or Donje Vecerska, if he travelled literally to the south of Vitez towards Kruscica, how far could he go?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A kilometre, a thousand metres, not much further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To the edge of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 433/1 could be provided to the witness, that's the first in the series of photographs which I believe you took? Do you recall when this was taken?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This was quite early on during my tour. I think maybe I had been a liaison officer four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask my colleague to read the banner or title which appears to the left or, actually, in the centre of the photograph so that it can be translated and then we can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, it says the municipal headquarters of Vitez HVO and to the right, the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you know what these signs said or meant during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was meant by municipal headquarters HVO, the left hand sign over this doorway?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As far as we were concerned, that was just the central headquarters where all units had some representative based, so we could access most people via the HVO hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was Colonel Blaskic the head of the municipal HVO or the municipal headquarters of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic, as far as we were concerned, was commander of Third OP zone as it was entitled later on and his headquarters was centred in the hotel Vitez so he was the senior commander involved in that municipal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding of why there were separate signs for the municipal HVO headquarters and the Vojne Policije HVO or military police of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I didn't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What element of the HVO Vojne Policije or military police were resident in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, the military police came under the same heading with the exception of small subunits like the Jokeri. The military police were a part of a battalion structure providing various aspects, military police units on the ground in the area of Vitez, part of which of their function was protection of the likes of Colonel Blaskic when on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question was, were you aware of what element of the military police were resident in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My understanding, sir, was that there were representatives of all elements of the military police in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said yesterday the commander of the Jokers was Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was his office in the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I never actually met him in the Hotel Vitez. The only character I met connected was the Jokeri and military police was the character I knew as Vlado, but on the occasion where the senior military police, commander Pasko Ljubicic, was overseeing a convoy delivery to Vitez and the Kruscica area, he emerged from the Hotel Vitez with Darko Gelic. I then assumed that having already met Vlado there, who I knew as part of the military police structure, that I assumed Pasko Ljubicic was also centred in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Jumping ahead for a moment, when you talked to several young soldiers at the Swiss chalet or bungalow, where did they tell you to go to find Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They just told me to go down to the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you to go to the police station, Mr. Whitworth?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, that was an assumption on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What do you mean that was an assumption on your part? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They had already told me that they were part of an elite military police unit, therefore, when they directed me to Vitez, I went to visit the civilian police first and then the Hotel Vitez where, as far as we were concerned, the military police were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So your current recollection is that no one at the bungalow told you to go to the civil police station, you just went there of your own accord; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The reason that was done was very simply I had made no introductions to the civil police. It was relatively early on in my tour, and I used my meeting with the military police as an excuse to turn up the civilian police and familiarise myself with the key personnel in there, which is obviously an important aspect of my job, in liaising with the people in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the police station, did you ask where Pasko Ljubicic's office was?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did not, sir. I just asked if I could speak to the senior military police commander and feigned that it was a mistake on my part that I actually turned up at the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever during your tour ask anybody else where Pasko Ljubicic's office was?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Exhibit 257 could be provided to the witness and, perhaps, placed on the ELMO? If you could examine that exhibit briefly. Do you recognise it as a schematic drawing of at least portions of the Hotel Vitez ground floor and, perhaps, -- I believe ground floor. The diagram is limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, take your time to look at the document. Since you are not familiar, it will take a minute or two to have a look at it, get to know it.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I hope people appreciate, it's a little difficult when walking around a concrete building to orientate yourself, so I'm just trying to do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I'm telling you to take your time, to familiarise yourself with the document before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me know when you have had sufficient time, Mr. Whitworth, to familiarise yourself with the document, okay?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: My recollection, sir, is slightly different from that, and the area which I met Colonel Blaskic and escorted Colonel Alastair to meet Colonel Blaskic was somewhere around this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, just to the left of the notation "stairs to warehouse"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't recall -- there were numerous doors. I don't know where most of them went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me -- have you completed your answer?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the notation in the centre of the diagram, "first company of active military police office" and then there's an arrow down below that to a box which is adjacent to something entitled "resting room"; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who the first company of the active military police was commanded by? Who was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that Pasko Ljubicic's job?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was aware, sir, has there were several units within the military police, and so let's say we addressed matters concerning any military police issue to Hotel Vitez, assuming that they would pass on the necessary information to the respective department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you already testified that Pasko Ljubicic was the battalion commander not the company commander of the HVO Vojne Policije?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does that say to you that the office of the first company of the acted military police would not have been Pasko Ljubicic's office?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not likely --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the witness said he doesn't know. If counsel is unhappy with that testimony, he can change the question but he said he does not know who was in that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, answer the last question clearly, the last question that Mr. Hayman asked, and then he will move on. Did you know, did you not know, to what extent did you know? Take your time.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I didn't know the person resident in that office, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Down across the street from the Hotel Vitez, do you see a box titled "civilian police"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that the location of the civilian police station to which you referred earlier, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Approximately, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Next to that box, do you see a box that says "one office Zvonko Vukovic, later Pasko Ljubicic"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does that, in any way, refresh your memory with respect to the location of Pasko Ljubicic's office?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Many of the meetings that I had in the Hotel Vitez took place in the reception area, and people were very reluctant, in fact, on very rare occasions only were we allowed into people's offices. The hotel Vitez, as far as I was concerned, was a place I could go and arrange to meet people. On the occasion I gave earlier, I met Pasko Ljubicic in the Hotel Vitez. I also met numerous other people in the Hotel Vitez after requesting to speak to them. On the occasion I visited the civilian police, I was directed to go to the Hotel Vitez and there are several other names in those boxes, Ivan Santic and Pero Skopljak which were, as far as I was aware, were not in the civilian police building, but were in the civil building which was to the rear of the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is a Prosecution exhibit, so I'm not reaching for it. I don't want to mislead you in that regard, if you disagree with the exhibit, so be it, but I don't want to you suggest that I'm suggesting to you that it's either accurate or inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then I think the proper suggestion should be to put it in its proper time frame which was up to the early part of April of 1993, which was what the witness testified concerning this exhibit and not during the time frame when this witness was in theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman and Mr. Kehoe, I know that your comments are very important, but the Judges will be able to evaluate the questions themselves. Each of us has his work to do. Mr. Hayman, please move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am moving to another question, Mr. President, gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Valenta and that you were told by Santic and Skopljak that Valenta would be the liaison officer to UNPROFOR; do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat that again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that I believe it was Mr. Santic and/or Mr. Skopljak informed you that Anto Valenta would be or was the liaison officer to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then please, the record, in some way, is not accurate. Can you tell us what did they tell you about Mr. Valenta?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: When I started my duties as the liaison officer, the first people that I met were Mayor Santic and Pero Skopljak, the local HDZ leader. After initially a few meetings with them, they said it would be of use to me and assist if I was to familiarise myself with characters in the Hotel Vitez and they arranged a meeting between myself and Anto Valenta, who was the senior political figure in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a more specific title for Mr. Valenta? You say he was the senior political figure. Did you know what his title or position was?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I can't recall that as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Approximately, when did you first meet him in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would say it was sometime before the middle of June, quite early on in my tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, I would guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After the fall of Travnik to the BiH army, on or about the 10th or 12th of June, or are you not sure?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would say it was before that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What do you use to find that date in time, your memory, or have you refreshed it with some reference in a document?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It's purely memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On Exhibit 257, can you indicate where you met Anto Valenta in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This is an unfamiliar layout to me, but I remember going off a corridor somewhere I thought was down here, into this area of the building, because there was quite clearly a window that looked somewhere out towards the back of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you're indicating up around where there's a legend, first floor offices, in that general area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In this area here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And, thereafter, did you have a series of meetings with him in the Hotel Vitez or only one meeting?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it might have been twice and then the third time I met him was arranging an escort to Kiseljak for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many times did you meet him in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the same month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't repeat the questions too much, Mr. Hayman. You've just asked the question. He said that he met him twice. Avoid references -- avoid too many references to this document which does date from 1993, after all. Let's get to the principal objectives, Mr. Hayman, to the essential points. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the Hotel Vitez, that was my question, how many times did you meet him in this office you've described and when, please?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it was twice and it was early on towards my tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever told that Anto Valenta took an office temporarily in the Hotel Vitez after he lost his office in Travnik due to the fall of Travnik in the first half of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was never aware, and to the best of my knowledge, the MILINFO people were never aware that he was based in Travnik. We always knew him as located in the Hotel Vitez. On numerous occasions, I saw his personal assistant in the Hotel Vitez, and whilst I didn't see Anto Valenta, I saw his personal assistant on several occasions around the time I met him twice in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Around that same time, you mean. You said in your first conversation with him that Mr. Valenta took the position that a particular area would be entirely Croat in ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you understand that position to be contrary to the terms of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan which was then being actively discussed, if not, in fact, agreed upon by at least two of the warring parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall which particular agreement, yes, but it was contravening what was being agreed to at higher levels, politically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there later points in time in your discussions with the civil authorities in Vitez, Santic, Skopljak, Valenta, where they indicated that they didn't care for the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and/or they didn't care for agreements reached by Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I had various conversations with Mayor Santic and on occasions he was quite adamant that the current plans were not going to work, but he was also fully aware of the fact that there was a need to keep Muslim and Croat communities integrated to a certain degree, and he was one of the people -- the mayor was one of the people I worked quite closely with early on in the tour. So there was agreement and disagreement depending on the time of day of the week, depending on what the particular level of tension was in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you not also perceive disagreements within the circle of civil authorities in Vitez; Santic, Skopljak and Valenta, they disagreed on issues such as those that you have been mentioning? Correct, at times?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall any as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You've just said that Mayor Santic was in favour of some degree of integration between the Croatian and Muslim communities. Is that a different perspective than that provided by Mr. Valenta when you met with him on the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was Mr. Valenta held in high regard by the towns people, that is, the ordinary persons of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I took it as so, based on his location in the Hotel Vitez, but he was not a local figure, so not particularly well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss Anto Valenta's views with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your presence, did Colonel Blaskic ever express such views, views of racial prejudice or animosity?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 80/8 could be provided to the witness? This, Mr. Whitworth, is one of a series of photographs of various persons walking, apparently, down a street or plaza, one of them being Anto Valenta. Did you take this picture?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When was it taken?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was taken, I can't remember the date, it was an organised movement of senior HVO and Croatian officials to Kiseljak and an attempt to negotiate some local arrangements at the U.N. headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So all these persons got together for the purpose of, first of all, I take it, being transported by UNPROFOR securely to Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that transport was necessary because Vitez was in an enclave surrounded by the BiH army at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the purpose of there being transported by the United Nations to Kiseljak was to engage in some type of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With whom, with the BiH army or with other civil leaders? Who were the parties involved?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: From my understanding, it was chaired by the U.N. representatives in Kiseljak, but there would be several key figures from the Armija and the Muslim communities in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any way to date the event? Can you give us a month, if not a date?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would say June, the June period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You suggested yesterday that Mr. Valenta had influence on military activity in Central Bosnia. Can you give the court an example of in what way or ways Mr. Valenta influenced military activity in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The assumption of his military involvement was based on the fact that his office, as far as we were concerned, was co-located with the senior military commanders of the area in the centre of Vitez. He was the senior political figure, and we assumed, therefore, that he had an influence over the policy and strategic decisions that were being made by the military commanders in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Those are assumptions. I asked for an example. Do you have an example to give to the court --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would ask the counsel to ask him questions and with regard to the witness, that counsel's editorialising or commenting on the witness's testimony, I would ask him to refrain from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Avoid comments, Mr. Hayman, if you want to make any. Let the witness have the time to answer. These are, of course, hypotheses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The record, Mr. President, my goodness, I don't think counsel's comments are well taken. The witness stated that they made an assumption, and I said thank you, those are assumptions. Can you give us an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, can you give the court an example, one example, during your six-month tour in Central Bosnia when Mr. Valenta influenced military activity in the region?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To my knowledge, I saw no example. I just restate the assumption that we made earlier which was based on our observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you described HVO communications capabilities. I would like to ask you two or three questions about that subject. Were you ever given a tour of the communications facility or room that provided communication support to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not an official tour, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where it was?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I walked into the room, I saw it was -- the communications, it was actually down some stairs, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this room in the Hotel Vitez or in the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This was in the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that where you think communications were based for the central operative zone of the HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that, sir. I just said I cited examples of types of communications I saw and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, please wait for the witness's answer and speak a little bit more slowly so that the interpreters can work more easily. And then the witness is asked to speak to the Judges when he answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be permitted to complete his answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I didn't interrupt him, Your Honour, with all due respect. The court did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counsel, I understand. I just ask that the witness be permitted to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, please, complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you asking for an apology from the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, do you have a further answer to give on that question?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do. To restate what I said earlier, I didn't actually claim to have been in the operational headquarters within Hotel Vitez, but just to give examples of the types of communications that I had seen in the various parts of the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any equipment in the Hotel Vitez that, in your judgement, was designed to provide secure communications capabilities to the commanders and the commander of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what is meant by the term "packet radio"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It's not a term I'm familiar with, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said you saw a satellite TV piece of equipment. By that, do you mean a dish that can be used to receive cable television, sometimes without paying a monthly fee?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, that type of equipment also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that what you mean, you did see such a dish?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Certainly if not on the actual hotel, up and down the Lasva Valley, I saw a couple of examples of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you also said something about a satellite phone or telephone. What did you see in that regard?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They appeared to have what was a telephone system, and I assumed it was a box, like, a briefcase box with a telephone, that is similar to ones I have seen before that don't require a land line, but simply wired up to an antenna system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could such equipment be either a radiophone or something else?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If Exhibit 433/7 could be provided to the witness, we're turning now, Mr. Whitworth, to the subject of helicopters. Can you tell us when you took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I can't. There were numerous instances where a helicopter landed in the Lasva Valley, and that could have been one of many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When did these helicopters first start coming to the Lasva Valley, what month, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would have said quite early on in June again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any way to date that, other than your recollection? Do you have any notations, reports, MILINFOSUMs you've reviewed to provide a date for when you saw the first helicopter come to the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, it's just memory. I know there was a constant low-level stream, maybe one every day, every two or three days, land for five minutes. A lot of them were night flights in the evening, so it would be 11, 12.00 at night. Because of the proximity of the BRITBAT location to the landing site near the quarry it was quite easy either to hear them or to see the small arms fire, particularly at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You always heard small arms fire when these helicopters came in, or no?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, you rarely hear the small arms fire. You just see if they're using tracer if they are firing at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This particular helicopter, did it land?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Whose helicopter was it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Our understanding is that it was an HVO, HV helicopter that had come from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, there was, again, supposition on our part. It didn't appear to be evacuating casualties, because we made regular checks on Nova Bila hospital. The situation didn't change there unless we assisted in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 434 could also be provided to the witness, please? When these helicopters landed, can you describe the way in which they landed?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they spiralled down very quickly because of the danger they are in as they approach the ground from BiH army troops in the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that a dangerous way to land a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Quite an uncomfortable way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the small arms fire directed against these helicopters. What happens when a helicopter is hit by a small arms fire?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Depending on where the small arms fire hits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What if it hits the engine?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It depends which bit of the engine it hits. Helicopters are pretty delicate pieces of equipment so they can't take too much damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You mean if they are hit in a place such as a functioning part of the engine --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A fuel line or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: -- or a fuel line, then they are going to crash; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the inhabitants will most likely be killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever ride on one of these helicopters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please speak a little bit more slowly, Mr. Hayman. The Judges do believe that if the helicopter is hit it might be dangerous. Let's try to get to the essentials, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have Exhibit 434 which indicates a helicopter pad with a circle around it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I said in that particular area, we weren't exactly sure. We never managed to get troops near it, but that was where the helicopter area came around, so it could quite easily have been on the other side of the ridge, in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could indicate where it could have been?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Several areas where it could have touched down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indicating to the upper right-hand corner of the ridgeline which also has a white road along -- near the top of the ridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you're not sure where the location was that these helicopters came closest to -- or it may have been outside of this circle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It may well have been, sir, yes. The helicopters were observed on numerous occasions during their landings and takeoffs by the guards who were constantly on duty outside BRITBAT location. As you can see from the proximity of the BRITBAT location, which is here, once the helicopter drops, it's difficult on the ground to actually see which particular feature it's dropping behind when it goes out of sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you personally ever see any of these helicopters land and touch the ground?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I didn't, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did any of these guards whom you've referenced, ever tell you that they personally saw a helicopter land or touch the ground?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, sir, once the helicopter disappears out of view behind one of these small ridges or hills, it's impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Am I correct that helicopters can also be used to drop supplies from a fairly low elevation and in that instance, the helicopter, in fact, doesn't land at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: By the very nature of the terrain, that would be an unnecessary thing to do. You can quite easily put a helicopter down there and be completely covered from view of Armija positions, load and unload whatever you like to, and then take off again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This circle on Exhibit 434 that says "helicopter pad," what was the pad made of concrete, asphalt?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I actually went up and recorded the area and found several large expanses of grass that quite easily could be used as a helicopter landing pad that had roads close by, which meant that pad area could be accessed by vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it there was no constructed pad in the sense of a concrete landing pad, perhaps with a large bright cross where people could see where they were going at night, that type of thing?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely not, sir. Bearing in mind, as I said earlier, the nature of the ground it would be quite easily to put lights on the ground, during a night landing, and nobody would have been aware of the fact because of the hills and the ridges surrounding that particular area. Only the person coming down from above would be able to see those markers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever participate in a helicopter medivac or a medical evacuation out of the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where did the helicopters come for such evacuations?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They used a local football field in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to talk about that for a moment, but one or two questions first. You said that BRITBAT had a belief that Colonel Blaskic left the theatre for some period of time for three to four weeks on one occasion. Can you tell us when that was? What month did BRITBAT form the opinion that Colonel Blaskic had left the theatre for approximately three to four weeks?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We saw earlier a photograph of several key HVO and Croat personalities being driven to Kiseljak in armoured vehicles. The return trip was organised some several days later, and there were numerous of those HVO Croat personalities that did not return in that transport, and yet reappeared in the Lasva Valley area sometime later. So they did not move via armoured vehicle provided by U.N. from Kiseljak, but, nevertheless, managed to re-enter the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was Colonel Blaskic one of those persons on this occasion, the occasion you're describing, that he went to Kiseljak with the U.N. but he didn't come back with the U.N.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't honestly recall whether that was the case, sir. There were eight armoured vehicles, and I didn't actually supervise the return journey, but the drivers actually recorded those people who were returned because they had a list to compare against those they had actually taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So those persons would be in U.N. and UNPROFOR records, lists of those persons?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would hope so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said a list was made?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My initial question was, you said BRITBAT formed an opinion collectively and individually, you yourself, that at one point Colonel Blaskic was out of the theatre for three to four weeks. Can you tell us when was that? Can you give us even a month, Mr. Whitworth? Was it after the Grbavica battle?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, these helicopter medivac's from Kiseljak. Let's turn to that. Was there one or more than one of these operations?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can only remember one, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know why the helicopters did not come to Vitez to pick up these seriously and critically wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Because of the danger of flying into the Lasva area posed by the armija on the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it these critically wounded persons were put in trucks or ambulances and driven to Kiseljak and then airlifted out?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It sounds simple, sir, but there is a lot more to it then that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't mean to suggest, in any way, that it was a simple matter. But they were transported by surface to Kiseljak and then helicoptered out?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the court over what -- what route did this ambulance convoy or truck convoy of wounded take to get to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We would transit through the Lasva Valley area, exiting around Busovaca and then going through the BiH areas and entering into the Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the medivac convoy go through Visoko or did it go through Kacuni and Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it was Visoko, the route we took.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's the long way, correct, going up around Visoko, rather than taking the direct road from Busovaca to Kiseljak through Kacuni and Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We might have actually used both, because there were a couple of evacuation, but only one of them involved the helicopters, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know why this convoy would have taken the long way around Visoko rather than the direct route from Busovaca to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, because we didn't have the support of the Armija in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're saying the Armija in the Kacuni/Bilalovac area would not let this medical evacuation convoy pass; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did any of the wounded, the seriously wounded individuals in this medical convoy, die on the trip, that is, on the surface trip?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You discussed the Convoy of Joy. Let's turn to that subject. This was approximately the 10th or 11th of June, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described an occasion when Colonel Blaskic came to a scene where civilians were obstructing the convoy and Mario Cerkez was somehow spotted in the crowd; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what Cerkez was doing at the scene? Could you tell?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, he was one of the people orchestrating the crowd's participation in delaying the convoy's movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was Colonel Blaskic's reaction when he saw that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic tried to attract Commander Cerkez's attention at the time, and reluctantly Cerkez came forward. There was some exchange, some conversation between them in which, as far as I could see, the tone of Colonel Blaskic's voice was obviously one of reprimand towards Commander Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that Colonel Blaskic had instructed Mr. Cerkez to obstruct this convoy or that, on the contrary, he had given no such instruction and he was displeased that Mr. Cerkez was engaged in such activity?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, he was expressing displeasure at what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said after this incident, you and Darko Gelic visited all the local militia commanders to reconstitute the trucks that had been in the Convoy of Joy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, not all the local militia commanders. We obviously aimed our activities at the areas we found the largest collection of vehicles, and we had to negotiate with the local commanders and the HVO soldiers who were responsible for supervising and guarding those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What local militia commanders did you visit in an attempt to reconstitute and free the convoy?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Carlo Grabovac and his name escapes me, but the battalion commander -- sorry, the HVO battalion commander, who was located near BRITBAT area, who was responsible for the quarry area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why was it necessary for you and Darko Gelic to go around and visit these people? Why couldn't Colonel Blaskic have simply issued an order to these local malitias telling them "Bring the trucks to this location. Reconstitute the convoy so it can go on its merry way."

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't know. Why couldn't Colonel Blaskic issue an order to that effect? That is what we asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What did he say? Did you discuss it with him?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I didn't discuss it with him personally, that's why Darko and Vanja ended up coming along with me, because we had been given assurances by Darko, allegedly from Colonel Blaskic, that everything would be okay and we would be able to remove the trucks. But, on my own, when I tried to collect all the trucks together to reform the Convoy of Joy, that wasn't allowed, so an order, obviously as far as we were concerned, hadn't been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have your interpreter on this odyssey visiting the local militias?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did indeed on the first day and on the second day, I used Vanja, who was the daughter of one of the staff officers in Hotel Vitez, as my personal interpreter as a way of saying this is a bona fide authorised act from the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did any of the interpreters interpret for you the conversations between Darko Gelic and the local militia commanders concerning the release of the convoy? What did Gelic tell them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, would you please look at the Judges when you answer. It's unpleasant to have the impression that this is a discussion between two other people. You are being asked questions but you have to direct your answers to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't recall any such conversations, conversations like that between Gelic and the local commanders usually took place in private. So I can't fulfil anything on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you present at any incidents involving the Convoy of Joy that involved either Dario Kordic or General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree with the statement that Mario Cerkez did not visibly accept Blaskic's orders? Do you agree with that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He complied with the orders, but it was with extreme reluctance on his part, and on numerous meetings with Cerkez, he was never -- rarely in agreement with Colonel Blaskic's intentions, but was, nevertheless, compliant when under pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In what way did he vary? Was he more conciliatory towards the BiH army or the Muslim community, or was he less conciliatory then the views being advocated by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He didn't express any views in that particular way. I think, really, his focus was more on the smaller, local issues in the Vitez/Lasva Valley pocket as opposed to the larger strategic issues of which we expected Colonel Blaskic to be more concerned with anyway. So I think it was difficult for Mario Cerkez to appreciate why Colonel Blaskic might have been doing what he was trying to do and disagreed with it at a local level. He also had a lot closer contact with the local population, so he was very, very concerned about his popularity in the Vitez area, Mario Cerkez, that is, and so would not do anything that would risk his popularity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you apprised that Colonel Blaskic was less concerned with his popularity in the local Vitez area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I don't have any thoughts on that particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was the source of these disagreements, of this resistance you're indicating there was on the part of Mr. Cerkez to direction or orders being given by Colonel Blaskic? Where was the rub?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, Mario was -- Mario's focus was more on local issues, not on the larger strategic ones up and down the Lasva pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you tell the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor in your written and signed statement of May 14th, 1997 that Cerkez did not visibly accept Blaskic's orders, page 7, third line?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would rephrase that and say that he did not visibly agree with Blaskic's orders, but, nevertheless, he carried them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you don't agree with your prior statement, and you would like to revise it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, what have you reviewed since you made this statement that refreshes your recollection or gives you further information that changes your view on that issue?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Since my initial interview which has refocused my attention on this subject, I have had time to think and dwell upon it and reflect. I came away from Bosnia with very lasting impressions about the relationships between people in the Lasva Valley area, and those have resurfaced since I started digging into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How long have you been in The Hague preparing your testimony for yesterday and today? How many days?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A couple of days during which time I have really read through the MILINFOSUMs which has helped me a great deal in putting things in chronological order. I had a lot of memories and recollections but it didn't make sense to me, chronologically speaking, but having referred to the MILINFOSUMs now, it's made sense to me, in terms of knowing why that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described Cerkez as the local militia commander, and I would like to ask you about what the brigades were made of. Would you agree that the HVO brigades were formed on a territorial principle?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In essence, one village would -- the men from one village would comprise a company or satnija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, since we have changed subjects. Perhaps we will take our break now. We will wait -- about how much longer do you plan to ask questions, Mr. Hayman? We're going to resume in about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have completed about one-third of my cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume in twenty minutes. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We were discussing the nature of the brigades, and I believe I had asked whether you would agree that, in general, the men in a particular village would provide the manpower for perhaps a company or satnija?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And then a group of villages adjacent to one another might combine several companies into a bojna or battalion?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The men in these HVO brigades, would you agree that they generally lived in their homes and did not live in military barracks?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that they had their weapons and uniforms, for the most part, in their homes when they were not actively on duty?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if these individuals served full time, generally, these local militia in the brigades, or did they, rather, have a certain period such as a week or two during the month where they were on duty, and the rest of the time they led their lives, whether it's tending the garden or having some other type of job?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Our impression was a little bit of both, depending on the proximity of the soldiers' homes to the front-line positions. But they obviously did duties as such. Whether that was a week on, a week off, I'm not quite sure about that, but I'm sure it was on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How is this territorial principle different from a professional army that would take conscripts, for example, from a larger geographic area, combine them and mix them, and put them in barracks. Can you compare the two? Are you able to?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A normal battalion would have a very large catchment area because not everybody is a soldier, obviously. They would be barracked separately and away from their homes all together as soldiers, and they would be centralised with their equipment and uniforms whilst in barracks and on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that the territorial nature of the HVO brigades was one reason that a brigade commander like Mario Cerkez was very concerned with local issues and problems, because he was from the local area and all of his men were from the local area; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you also agree that as a result, in the case of Mario Cerkez, the name "Cerkez" had more influence around the Vitez pocket than did the name "Blaskic"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would agree with that as far as the local civilians were concerned. If I was talking to people living in and around the Vitez area, for the most part, Mario Cerkez was their key military reference point. He was the person, being a local person, that they knew best out of the military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with the statement that Cerkez did not seem to accept subordination of or from Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with the statement, "Mario Cerkez. He was the commander of the Vitez HVO troops, and did not seem to accept subordination of Colonel Blaskic"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm reading from page 3 of your signed statement in the middle under "Personalities: Mario Cerkez." If you disagree with this statement now, can you tell the court what examples or other material in the MILINFOSUMs or other material you have studied this week has caused you to now disagree with your statement of May 14, 1997 in that regard? Or, on reflection, if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you please repeat the last thing you said? I didn't quite follow. What was that part of the statement that you are referring to, that you're trying to have the witness explain why he retracted his first statement and has now made another one. I'm looking at the transcript, but I'm not quite sure I understand what the witness said about that. Would you mind going back over that again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. It's a slightly unusual use of English, so I'm not surprised the translation is difficult as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Page 3, middle of the page, "Personalities: Mario Cerkez. He was the commander of the Vitez HVO troops, and did not seem to accept subordination of Colonel Blaskic."

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Would you like me to clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you tell us, again, whether you agree or disagree, and if you disagree, what is it that has caused you to change your views?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I agree with that statement. If I was to visit Mario at the cinema, I am not under the influence of Colonel Blaskic or anybody else in the HVO, if I went to him and said, "I would like to do this" or "to do that," he would say, "No, it's not happening," or "No, I don't agree. I will not allow that to happen." I would then go to the Hotel Vitez and petition Colonel Blaskic, usually through Darko Gelic, as to what I was trying to do and why I was trying to do it. Usually, after a period of time, they would say, "Okay, you should be able to do that now." I would then attempt to move to wherever it was or deliver whatever it is I was trying to do, and not being able to achieve that, I would then return to Mario Cerkez, as it was him who directly commanded the troops in the Vitez area who would stop me doing what I was trying to do. And I would say to Mario, "This has been issued from Colonel Blaskic. Can you make sure that your soldiers on the ground are informed as such, and that will allow me to complete whatever task I'm trying to undertake." Mario's usual response would be, "I have received no such order. Show me a piece of paper with the order issued on it." On several occasions, he was quite adamant that he did not agree with the decision, but when confronted, as I think I gave an example earlier, by Colonel Blaskic in the presence of Colonel Blaskic, then Mario would follow suit. Mario Cerkez would comply with Colonel Blaskic's orders, as was the case with the Convoy of Joy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you give the court any other examples with respect to which Mario Cerkez said, "No, I won't do it. I have not received an order from Blaskic"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall any specific examples, but my entire time during the tour of Bosnia was spent trying to move aid in and out of the area, and there were numerous examples, numerous occasions, when I was rebuffed by the likes of Mario in an attempt to move into, say, a Muslim area or into Stari Vitez, for example, on the basis that Mario said he did not receive an order or he was not willing to comply with that, that was not part of what was being agreed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Am I correct then that on repeated occasions, Mario Cerkez told you he had not received an order for free passage of UNHCR aid convoys within the Vitez enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described an incident with three young Croat boys, apparently in Kruscica, and an attempted exchange involving two wounded and so forth. Do you know what the three young boys were being held for? What was the purpose of their detention or imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were actually picked up by a BiH patrol in the area of Kruscica. Their parents had actually told me that they had been sent out to collect wood. When I met Sivro Sifet, the Armija commander who was in possession of these children, he said they had been picked up wandering around the woods by one of the Armija patrols and returned to Kruscica area. All three of the children were well looked after and had a good relationship with the civilian police officers who were actually overseeing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That explains why they were picked up. Why were they being held, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
