utterances.text: As far as I was aware, there are, actually, no facilities in place, unless it's through the likes of myself or the ICRC, for one side to exchange people with the other side. So they couldn't, basically, walk up to the front-line with three kids, pass them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it that was true with respect to both sides, that if there were people who wanted to cross the front-line, they might be detained because there was no safe way to cross the front-line, other than through an organised exchange of some sort; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I presume there was a lot of suspicion attached by either side to anybody attempting to cross the front-line, but, yes, what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the two wounded that were taken to Cerkez's headquarters? What ultimately happened to them? Did they get out? Did they get the treatment they needed?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: On that particular occasion, yes, they were released to my sergeant who escorted them to Zenica, and I returned from Kruscica into Vitez with the three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is this incident a good example of the kind of tit-for-tat provocation and incidents which occurred on both sides of this conflict?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It is typically the type, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You spoke of your conversation with a number of young soldiers at the bungalow, members of the Jokers. Let's turn to that now, please. Were they better equipped than the territorial militia or the brigade militias within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, they were, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you how they got their equipment?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No. Obviously, under the circumstances, people are very suspicious when you start questioning them intensely on where they come from, where their supplies come from, et cetera, et cetera. It's a very delicate discussion. So, no, I didn't ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit D138 could be provided to the witness and put on the ELMO, we are concluded with Exhibit 434.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Whitworth, why don't you take a moment to look at this portion of a MILINFOSUM dated 10 August 1993, and I would like to direct your attention to the second line which states: "The Jokers are a subunit within the Fourth BN of the HVO MP." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President, there is a French translation of this exhibit. Just for your assistance, I note that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I think I'm doing all right with the interpreters, unless the registrar gives it to me. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was Pasko Ljubicic the commander of the Fourth Battalion of the HVO police. Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was my understanding, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding of where the First, Second, and Third Battalions of the military police served?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding of to whom these four military police battalions report, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it might have been to Mostar or somewhere like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about the incident in Rijeka with the displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 56, it's a large exhibit, if I could see it first. If Exhibit 435 could be provided to the witness right now, we will see if we can conclude this area with the smaller exhibit. For the record, 435 is a portion of Exhibit 56, but it borders the northern edge or the upper edge of the photograph. So there's no additional portion of the photograph above what is depicted at the top of Exhibit 435.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn, Mr. Whitworth, how these displaced persons came to be in the area of the green circle on Exhibit 435?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were DPs from, what I understood, the Turbe area who had been moved into the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn when they came to the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where was the front-line from this photograph? Could you indicate on the ELMO with the pointer, if you're able? I understand it may be off the photograph, but can you give us some indication of how it ran?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Probably somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could leave that pointer in that position, for the record, the pointer is running along the right-hand side of the photograph with the words "Portion of Exhibit 56" at the bottom at a slight angle intersecting the upper right-hand corner of the exhibit. Do you see the houses which are along a road and are, in fact, closer to the front-line than the houses in the green circle? If you can look at where I'm pointing - I have a copy of the exhibit in my hand - you may be able to see it from the distance where you are.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Firstly, the front-line is probably a little bit further in that direction to where I have put the marker. The other thing I would say is this was the only photograph that had the area closest on it. That green circle was the approximate area. It was actually somewhere along this track that the collection of houses were located where these people were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you: If you look where I'm pointing, do you see this row of houses along this road which runs parallel to the right-hand edge on the upper right-hand portion of the exhibit, which is 435?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who lived in those houses?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were within the Croat area of the Lasva Valley. I'm not quite sure who was occupying them or if they were occupied at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever go there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I visited that area on one occasion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there Croat families living in those houses at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Specifically those houses there, I cannot recall. I remember on that road out somewhere meeting a local HVO militia soldier who was very aggressive towards me when I was trying to transit towards the Muslim area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's generally correct, is it not, that there were Croat families living in virtually all of these houses around the area of the green circle on Exhibit 435?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Quite possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were they being used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think you obviously missed the point I made earlier. The green circle is not necessarily the location. That was the only map I was given to indicate the area where the houses were situated. I did, indeed, provide a photograph earlier which showed empty houses with mines across the road, and that was the area I clearly remember as being adjacent to where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you speak a little bit more slowly for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: So not specifically that group of houses, but an area up that particular track, and that was the only available photograph to which I marked on the closest thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you determine who, if anyone, was actually trying to keep these displaced persons in the houses they were in? Were they locals, local soldiers, local civilians, the Vitez brigade, someone else? Who was trying to do this?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: On the occasion that I tried to allow them free passage out of the area, there were local militia and a military police vehicle with three occupants all quite clearly labelled as military police that stopped my escort of these people out of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if, on that occasion, were they acting on anyone else's orders or were they acting on self initiative?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that to say you don't know?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can not recall at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were any of these displaced persons injured in any attacks or fighting between the HVO and the BH army that you know of?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you about Darko Kraljevic. You said you met him on or about the 11th or 12th of June on an occasion when there was shelling by the BiH army of what portions of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The actual town centre area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was in the town centre? What was the target of that mortar attack?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to say. It could be it was just a shelling of the town centre area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it you're unaware of any military targets in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Other than the OP zone, Third OP zone headquarters, which was actually hit during the barrage, the only other place might have been the ammunition factory, but I don't think they were rounds falling in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Vitezit or Slobodan Princip factory was a kilometre or two outside the centre of town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What else was happening on the 11th or 12th of June, 1993? Was the HVO withdrawing from Travnik because the BiH army had taken over Travnik on about the 12th of June, 1993, within a day or two. I'm suggesting there was action going on in Travnik which either had led to the fall or the imminent fall of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I find that very difficult to recall specific times. It was an extremely busy time of year, and there were several major actions taking place on and around the same time. I'll be honest and say that they all sort of blur into one, as far as I'm concerned. I can't recall specific dates, other than generally saying that they all happened on or around the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I apologise if I am asking you to repeat any of your testimony yesterday, but I didn't understand completely. Who stopped you? What soldiers from what unit stopped you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: With respect to which specific event?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The event when Kraljevic put the gun to your face?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were HVO militia, local Croatians, and there were the battalion commander and his soldiers in the crowd of people who were the immediate barrier to the warriors, along to the mines that were placed across the road transiting past Vitez. Likewise, those HVO militia, as well as Kraljevic and his troops and civilians, were also gathered around the vehicles in the centre of Vitez on that particular evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this a highly agitated crowd?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was a very agitated crowd under the circumstances. It was a very emotive time. If I remember correctly, the Convoy of Joy was also trying to transit through the area, and there were shells falling in the centre of Vitez area. People were being injured while this was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How were Kraljevic's Vitezovi soldiers dressed? What kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall them being any different to the other members of the local militia. It was dark, obviously. There was no street lighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Kraljevic, apparently, told you he would or might kill you because he believed UNPROFOR was assisting the BiH army. Were you convinced by his threat that he held that belief at that time, that he, in fact, believed that UNPROFOR was assisting the BH army?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, I was not in a position to ignore what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, at the same time, you learned that there were one or more ECMM, EC monitors, in the basement of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember who they were, what monitors were there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was an English chap who is an ex-army officer. I think there was an Italian gentleman, large, rotund, but, nevertheless, jolly chap with a big black moustache. I can't remember his name. He was very approachable, amenable. I think there was an older gentleman, bald, slimmer build. The names, specifics, in that respect, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there HVO also taking cover in the basement of the Hotel Vitez with these EC monitors?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was reasonably happy with the situation of the ECMM. As far as I was concerned, they were not being held as hostages but were taking refuge in the Hotel Vitez for their own protection. The HVO seemed quite happy with that. The ECMM were regular frequenters of the Hotel Vitez, obviously, with it being the centre of HVO operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it a fair statement, in your view, that Darko Kraljevic was worshipped by the local Croat community in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think the phrase I used at the time was "feared and revered," and that's how I think he was looked upon by the local people. He was, obviously, a very effective military commander, but also he was very unpredictable, unstable. They were quite fearful of him. They were very wary of his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He was an extremely violent personality; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I saw nothing to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had a rank?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He called himself -- he was a colonel, as in on par with -- I correct myself. I don't recall him actually having a rank, not that he referred to himself, but he might have been referred to by others, by members of the civilian population, in some particular way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit D73 could be provided to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could just take a moment to look at that and tell us if that refreshes your recollection as to whether Darko Kraljevic held himself out as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: D73, it can be put on the ELMO, although I'm not sure if that's the English translation or the BSC.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you would direct yourself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This exhibit was not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't recall, Mr. President. I'm going to ask the witness if it refreshes his recollection. If the exhibit could be moved up so the signature line appears - this is the English translation - if it could be moved up slightly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is an English translation of an order which you also have the BCS copy of, and it's signed, by order, "Colonel Darko Kraljevic." Does that refresh your recollection in any way with respect to any encounters you may have had with Kraljevic in which he may have held himself out as having a certain rank?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can you just clarify what it is you're asking me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If, in any encounters, Kraljevic held himself out to you as a colonel, as having the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I never addressed him formally, and I can't recall any of his troops referring to him in such a light either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How did his troops refer to him?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: "Darko."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We're concluded with those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were shown a BBC tape of the exploding trenches. Do you know how the BBC came to be present at this event?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was actually a home video filmed by Kraljevic himself, to my knowledge, to the best of my knowledge, provided by him to the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When then was the BBC tape made; do you know? Was it made on the day of the explosion or was it a retrospective piece made a week or ten days later or do you know?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: You would have to ask them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it BRITBAT had no advance notice, to your knowledge, of this explosion in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Whose initiative was it; do you know?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Who initiated the plan and executed the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't know, no. I know Darko was responsible for -- boasted to me that he had been responsible for initiating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's what he told you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: When I say "initiating it," I mean actually planting the explosives, pressing the button, the actual on-the-ground execution of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What did he say in that regard? Did he say "I did it" or "I initiated it"; do you remember what he said?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall the specific conversation, but he said, "I'm responsible for that. I've blown up those trenches." He didn't intimate whether -- I can't recall whether he intimated it was a command decision on his part or whether he was just saying that he was responsible for the action itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The BBC narrator says on this tape "Darko Kraljevic promises a fierce defence of the Vitez pocket." Do you recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you find it odd that Darko Kraljevic is speaking to the world, to the international press, about his defence of the Vitez pocket, or do you find that consistent with his view of himself and of his role in the Vitez enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I find that consistent with his opinion about himself. He was a very egocentric character, as I think I said earlier, enjoyed press coverage and a lot of attention. He was quite happy to put himself to the fore as this elite HVO special forces commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that wherever he was, he held himself out as being in charge?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Wherever he was on the ground, I would say yes. As far as the local militia and battalion commanders were concerned, if he was there, then he obviously was quite a key figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of any examples in which Darko Kraljevic did not want to do something and yet he did it because Colonel Blaskic either asked or attempted to order him to do it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can you give me an example of what that might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, if Blaskic spoke to Kraljevic and said, "We need some of your men at the front-line." Kraljevic said, "No, we don't want to go to the front-line," and Blaskic said, "I order to you send 20 men to the front-line at Poculica," and Kraljevic did it, sent the men. Can you think of any examples wherein Kraljevic didn't want to do something but did it because Blaskic asked or ordered him to do it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Kraljevic's Vitezovi were approximately 20 to 30 in strength, and their role, as such, would not have encompassed that type of activity. They were ample HVO troops who were available should that type of circumstance arisen and that Colonel Blaskic would have had at his command to task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand what you said. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Certainly, sir, sorry. The Vitezovi were a group 20 to 30 in strength, and their function within the HVO, as we saw it, was not to assist in the defence of front-line positions. So the circumstances, when Colonel Blaskic would have had to order Darko Kraljevic to do those things, never actually existed. Colonel Blaskic had plenty of other troops and units which were more specifically directed to do tasks like that. I cannot think of a set of circumstances when Kraljevic would have had the opportunity to refuse an order from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you think of any examples in which Kraljevic wanted to do something and didn't do it because Blaskic either asked or ordered him not to?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think the same applies. I can't see circumstances when any of the military activity that the Vitezovi were involved in would not be of benefit to the strength of the HVO position in the Lasva Valley. So I don't think those circumstances would have arisen either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you can't think of any examples, as you say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you described another individual, Zuti, as a local criminal. Did you have encounters with Zuti?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I met him very briefly on one occasion, and that was a very fleeting meeting. My only real knowledge of Zuti was regular accounts from the liaison officer for the Novi Travnik area who, obviously, I spent a lot of time with at the end of every day, exchanging stories and tales of characteristics that we had met. That's my only real recollection of the character Zuti.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit D135 could be retrieved and provided to the witness on the ELMO while I ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree from the information you received that Zuti had a great deal of influence in the Bila and, at least portions of, the Travnik region?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He was certainly a very active character, but from what Captain Hay Angus told me, he wasn't active in any great military sense, other than having a seemingly endless supply of weapons, a ready supply of cache, vehicles, and the like. I think he was -- he gave me the impression he was an opportunist who was taking advantage of the circumstances in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Exhibit D135 is a memorandum by Colonel Duncan relating, in paragraph 3, a conversation that Colonel Duncan had with Colonel Blaskic wherein, among other things, it is said in the middle of paragraph 3: "It would appear that Zuti has considerable influence with the people of the Lasva Valley, whereas Blaskic has not, as proved by the events of the Convoy of Joy where Blaskic proved to be nothing more than a puppet commander ignored by the locals." Were you present at this meeting with Colonel Duncan and Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't recall being so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the meeting with Colonel Duncan?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that during your tour of duty, for the most part, the HVO fought a defensive war attempting to preserve the Vitez enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the HVO, none the less, lose a significant amount of territory of that enclave, during your tour, to the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: You're referring to Travnik; is that what you're referring to in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Travnik would be one area but not the only areas?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're saying that the HVO considered Travnik theirs before it fell to the BiH, rather than being a multi-ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why don't I rephrase the question and we will try to get back to that format. Once confrontation lines are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please ask your questions clearly, because in a little while we're going to have the witness asking you questions. Be more direct, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's why I'm going to reformulate the question. The witness's question was a good one. I concede that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: From the point that confrontation lines or frontlines were formed in the April and/or May time period when you arrived, are you able to say whether those lines moved in such a manner that the area under HVO control shrunk or enlarged or remained the same during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's difficult. When we took over, as you will be aware of the tour before ours, there were no actual frontlines between the Croat and Muslim communities. It was not for some considerable period of time after we had arrived that these frontlines started to actually take shape. I would conclude that by saying I would -- from the point of when we decided where those frontlines approximately lie, the HVO lost no appreciably large territory during our tour. They had minor losses - nothing that would be considered major in terms of the area of ground - but they lost a few strategic ones like the Zacilja point that overlooked the Lasva Valley, but not substantially large in terms of ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The beginning point of the time period you're evaluating is approximately when?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: From the middle of the tour onwards, the last three, four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: August on, something like that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: From August on, the frontlines were relatively stable; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were some minor incursions and counterattacks, regular exchanges, frontlines moved a little bit. But from my recollection, it didn't move in any appreciably large amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 433 could be provided to the witness, and if you could examine subexhibit numbers 13 and 14 which are, I believe, pictures taken at the -- one of them, at least, at the Nova Bila hospital. I believe this is 433-13 on the ELMO. You took this photograph, as I recall; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Around the middle of the tour. I spent quite a lot of time at Nova Bila hospital, and I think I would have said probably a little bit earlier than that. General Petkovic's visit was an attempt to get our support to allow HVO, HV helicopters or helicopters to come into the Lasva Valley to evacuate casualties. I think that's a little bit before the middle of the tour, towards the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this around the Convoy of Joy incident, around the 10th of June, 1993, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't say, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When Petkovic came to meet with the U.N. in the Vitez enclave, how did he get there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, he was brought there from Kiseljak by a U.N. vehicle. I think it was one of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Stari Vitez, let's discuss that subject briefly. Would you agree that at the beginning of your tour, Stari Vitez was well supplied with stockpiles of weapons and explosive devices?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I ever saw. They did boast that there had been a cache there when the Croat and Muslim population were working together before it became a tripartite confrontation in the area, but I never saw any evidence of that. In fact, I did see evidence of plenty of improvised grenades, and the weapon systems that they did have were very old, quite primitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you then if you agree with the statement that you made on page 6 of your prior written, signed statement, wherein you said: "As an enclave, Stari Vitez was fairly well supplied (initially) with stockpiles of weapons and improvised explosive devices." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Initially, I think that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you said "initially," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I often questioned Sefkija about how he could maintain, under Stari Vitez, how he could maintain and resist the action of the HVO from Vitez. He explained to me that in Stari Vitez, there had been a weapons cache because it was initially like a local militia headquarters in there, that both the Croat and the Muslim populations had actually centred and stockpiled various resources there, and, fortunately for them, that had been there when the relationship between the Croat and Muslim populations broke down, that they had that to fall back on and maintain their position. That was the situation, as far as I was concerned, as far as he explained it to me, when, during the Cheshire's tour, the relationship broke down between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is true that Djidic never admitted to you that they had a means to resupply Stari Vitez with materiel; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He never admitted a resupply method. I had never seen any evidence of stockpiled weapons, and the intelligence officer, the MILINF officer, and I often deliberated on if they were resupplying, how they could have gone about that. It would have been very difficult for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You believed, did you not, that the BiH army in Stari Vitez had to be receiving some type of military resupply to be able to sustain their defence of Stari Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I thought that was a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you think, and I'm quoting from your statement six or seven lines down: "My colleagues and I thought that supplies must have been getting through to the enclave in some form, but we never saw any evidence of this whatsoever." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that because, among other things, there was no munitions factory in Stari Vitez to produce munitions locally?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct. There was no facility in there, as far as I was aware, that could do that. It was actually an extremely small pocket, maybe 500 metres in diameter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you also suspicious on this point because you knew, as a trained soldier, that without resupply, an army will run out of needed items; it's simply a matter of time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's common sense. I was about to say, but regardless of any investigation that we made, we never actually found out any method of resupply, other than that one minor incident where they probably managed to smuggle several hundred rounds in, as I recounted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the HVO generally shared your belief that somehow, someone was re-supplying Stari Vitez with military materiel?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were accusations and counter-accusations on all parts from every faction involved, that one side was being favoured by organisations in supplying people with aid and weapons. So, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were these suspicions on the part of the HVO directed at the only entities that did have access into Stari Vitez at the time, which was UNPROFOR and certain humanitarian relief agencies?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct. They were directed at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it also correct that upon expression of these suspicions, UNPROFOR, understandably, and its personnel took strong offence?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think the first time you get that accusation, then you would be offended, because you are there doing what you think is a worthwhile job to the best of your ability. But that accusation came with such regularity that it became commonplace, and we just ignored it and got on with what we were trying to do. Initially, for a few minutes, offence, but after that, for the rest of the six months, it was just accepted as the norm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You would agree, though, I take it, that these HVO suspicions, they were rational, they were based on rational facts?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think anybody under the circumstances would have probably said the same thing. I didn't hold that against the HVO at all. We did go to whatever lengths were possible and that we were allowed to instil some confidence in them that we were trying to do the job to the best of our ability and they were unbiased and neutral on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You related the incident in which you, unknowingly and unwittingly, transported a certain amount of rounds of ammunition into Stari Vitez. You had collected these boxes of purported medical supplies from the UNHCR warehouse in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this the same warehouse, UNHCR warehouse in Zenica, where UNHCR food was delivered upon coming to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was the same warehouse that packed food for all the Lasva Valley area, Muslim and Croat communities alike, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Under whose control was this warehouse?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the date or month of this incident?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Prior to this incident, on how many occasions had you or other members of BRITBAT been asked to transport boxes of medical supplies or other supplies from this warehouse into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We were asked quite regularly to move things in, but it was common practice to refuse and encourage the respective organisation to make a journey and delivery, as was required, rather than us doing it. We tried to keep ourselves -- use the correct agencies and organisations, rather than taking over their role and, obviously, it detracted us from doing what we were trying to do on the ground in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many prior occasions had you escorted or transported these types of supplies, medical or food aid, into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think that was the second time I ever did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: These items were routinely transported into Stari Vitez by UNHCR itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, under my supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After you saw the BiH army soldier unpacking the rounds from the medical supply boxes, did you try and get the rounds back or did you conclude that that was not feasible or not appropriate?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Both, I think. I didn't feel it was appropriate, and the boxes were already broken open. My immediate reaction was to go to see Commander Sefkija and express my displeasure of what exactly had happened, as I think I said earlier, that he had sort of let me down and betrayed my trust, because I had obviously put myself out to do this for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What did commander Djidic say to you when you told him that you felt he had betrayed your trust?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He shook his shoulders. He didn't say a lot and he said these things are necessary and at that point I left very shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After the incident, did you report it up the chain of command within BRITBAT?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, yes, I reported to the MILINFO people that that was what actually happened, and I think I spoke to the UNHCR liaison officer as well, Captain Hancock so he could pass the information on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it written up in a MILINFOSUM report or another report?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I haven't seen one. I can't recall, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it reported to Colonel Duncan, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I personally didn't report it to him. I don't know whether he actually was aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Mark Bower occupy a position whereby he would have or did come to have this information?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would like to think that he did have the information. I can't recall having a specific conversation with him and telling him about it. That was the whole purpose of feeding information to the MILINFO so we all could be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you or anyone else within BRITBAT inform UNHCR of this matter?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the course of your conversations with Commander Djidic, did he tell you that Stari Vitez was well-supplied with cellars that could be used to store a large amount of military supplies?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't remember him specifically using those words, other than intimating that they did have the facility to store large quantities, and that he did actually say, as I think I said earlier, that they had a cache of militia stores that were a remnant before the breakdown of relationships between the Croat and Muslim communities, and that Stari Vitez was well equipped with cellars and that is where it was all stored and stashed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When he referred to cellars, did you understand him to refer to cellars in private homes or residences?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's all there were in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the dynamics between the HVO and the BiH army when there would be an attack or some provocation towards Stari Vitez. Do you agree that when the HVO did attack Stari Vitez, there would be stiff resistance from the BiH army in Stari Vitez and Commander Djidic would call in mortar fire on Vitez from ABiH positions in Kruscica, to the south, and from the 325th Brigade position north of Vitez, which would result in the attack being called off?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I said that Commander Sefkija had communications to 325 Brigade area and Kruscica, and that as far as Stari Vitez is concerned, it was a local exchange. They only had resources within their own territory, but they could fire back at the HVO and I'm not aware whether Commander Sefkija had the power to order artillery or mortar fire from either Kruscica or 325 Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To ensure that I'm paraphrasing your prior statement accurately, why don't you look, as I read to you, from page 6 of your statement, two-thirds of the way down in the paragraph entitled "Stari Vitez," and let me ask you if you agree with the precise way it is phrased in your statement. "The ABiH commander in Stari Vitez was Sefkija and he had communications with commander 325th Brigade on the hills above Vitez towards Zenica. Sefkija saw the level of command opposing him as being Cerkez, i.e., brigade level. When attacks on Stari Vitez came, these would be met with stiff resistance from within the enclave, and would also quickly be supported by mortar fire being directed at Vitez town from ABiH positions in Kruscica, to the south, and ABiH 325 Brigade positions, to the north." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I agree with the first part. Stiff resistance was met for the most part from within Stari Vitez. The regularity with which these flare-ups occurred, having now a bit more of a clearer recollection, I think the likelihood of mortars being called in onto Vitez by action on Stari Vitez is very small, but because it happened, these flare-ups occurred regularly, I can fully appreciate that repeated pressure from Sefkija on to 325 or Kruscica brigades, they might have responded on the odd, one or two occasions, by doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it also correct that after the mortar fire came in "The attack on Stari Vitez would then be called off by Cerkez." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As he was the brigade commander on the ground, that was just interpretation on my part, he would have been under direct control of the troops on the frontlines surrounding Stari Vitez, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Lastly, do you agree with the next sentence: "Sefkija did not assess the attacks to be commanded by Blaskic's level of command but from Cerkez at brigade level."

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, that was his assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, did you become familiar with the offers made by the Croat community in Vitez to the citizens of Stari Vitez to temporarily evacuate Stari Vitez and get out of the war zone?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of those offers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether the BiH army disseminated those offers to the civilian population in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I personally carried that message to Sefkija on some of the occasions it was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that was on multiple occasions, was it not, that that offer was made?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Multiple, I would say, probably two or three times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether Commander Djidic ever made a sincere effort to relay that message to the civilian population in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were all aware of that offer, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there any reason, to your knowledge, why the BiH army would have wanted civilians to stay in Stari Vitez and not evacuate?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The people occupying Stari Vitez were local people, people who had lived in Vitez and the Stari Vitez area, probably, all their lives, as were the people in Grbavica. They were being asked to give up their homes. They were a local militia in the same way the HVO defending their respective bit of the trenches were local. So what was being asked of them was to leave their homes and to effectively remove any Muslim population from the Lasva Valley area. Sefkija and all his subordinate commanders and the people I spoke to were determined that it was their home and they were going to stay there and did not want to take up the offer. And had they taken up that offer, it would have just gone further down the road to achieving Anto Valenta's initial impression that he gave me, which was removing all other ethnic groups, other than Croats, from the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It would have exposed the BiH army in Stari Vitez to a military action that would not have risked disproportionate civilian casualties; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Could you explain that again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Had the Muslims civilians left Stari Vitez, it would have exposed the BiH army in Stari Vitez to a possible military offensive by the HVO, unconstrained by the danger of excessive civilian casualties in Stari Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Who are you classifying as civilians at this point in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, why don't you tell us. Was everyone in Stari Vitez contributing towards the BiH army war effort?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were very few people wearing uniforms in Stari Vitez, and like most the population in the Lasva Valley, they had arms of one form or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe Commander Djidic told us there were 250 BiH army soldiers and police in Stari Vitez. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I know that one of the civilian police officers was resident there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does 250 sound about right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: 250 males, about the fighting age, armed with small arms, sounds about right to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were all such males in Stari Vitez active in the military defence of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Everybody was active in the defence of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're saying men and women were active in the defence?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I saw women bearing arms as well, if they were of that ilk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, certainly there were some old people and young children in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So let's call them the civilians. We'll exclude everyone else, for purposes of this question.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'd also like to make it clear that I'm not saying the circumstances are any different in Stari Vitez when compared to the local Croat population. The circumstances were difficult for everybody, and people were living on the front-line, be they Croat or Muslim. And so many people just bared arms if they were able-bodied enough, but didn't necessarily wear a uniform. And as to whether you could call them soldiers or not, that's semantics, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The entire population of the region was armed, was it not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And not just with small arms, but there were explosives to be found among the general population, et cetera; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 252 could be retrieved, and while that is being done, I have one last question on Stari Vitez. If the old people and the children had left, then would the BiH army in Stari Vitez have faced the possible attack by the HVO unconstrained by the risk to the HVO of a large number of civilian casualties in Stari Vitez? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I agree with that. They would have been unconstrained in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Exhibit 252 was shown to you. Did you take this picture?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly when and where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was taken towards the end of the tour. It was probably one of the biggest body exchanges I've done during the tour. It's actually near -- it's on the road to Kruscica, on the HVO front-line. That's Carlo Grabovac stood there. The local battalion commander and on his right with his back to us is one of the local Croat people. That's the plastic sheet, is a sniper screen so people can walk across the road on the Croat side without being sniped up from the BiH frontlines. You can see past the sniper screens, there are mines across the road so the Croats can control exactly who goes into the Kruscica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So this is near the front-line in Kruscica and the white sheet is to protect military and civilians against sniper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were these sheets also to be found in the area of Vitez abutting Stari Vitez, these types of sheets outside of doorways, between buildings, so that people could move around and would not be hit or they would be less likely to be hit by snipers in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: For the most part, all the people were withdrawn into the centre of the Stari Vitez pocket, so there was cover from sniper fire afforded by the buildings, because there were several layers of buildings on the outside that had been damaged during the attack. And so, for the most part, unless crossing a major road, these things weren't absolutely necessary, because the close quartered nature of the buildings in old Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You're referring to old Vitez. What about Vitez proper, across or at the Croat edge of the front-line in Vitez facing Stari Vitez; were these types of sheets also draped, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the sniping activity in the region frequently a tit-for-tat type of act, retaliation, retaliation type of exchange?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was indeed so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to suspend the hearing and we will resume at 2.30. Court stands adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will now resume. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If Exhibit 433-16 could be retrieved and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now, Mr. Whitworth, to the subject of Bebes, that is, this particular type of explosive device and its use in Vitez. How many Bebes did you personally see fall in Stari Vitez and cause damage or injury?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I didn't actually see any. The only one I saw or the couple I saw were ones that hadn't gone off and that were shown to me by Sefkija's soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever present at the scene when one of them was fired, that is, launched towards Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, but I did observe the firing plates in the vicinity in Vitez adjacent to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where were the firing plates on the occasion or occasions that you saw them?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were in a couple of gardens -- one was in a garden, rather, and the other several ones and parts thereof were in the welding shop, which is out in the southern side of the town of Vitez where they were actually made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The ones that were in gardens --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The one that was in the garden I saw, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The one that was in a garden, how far was that garden from the Croat edge of the front-line between Vitez and Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: 500, 600 metres. It wasn't actually aimed at anything in particular. It just sat there adjacent to a house. So it would, in all likelihood, have been moved to a firing location as and when it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, the image on photograph Exhibit 433-16, who told you that that damage was caused by a Bebe?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was told to me by the troops on the ground. When I examined it closely, there was a lack of shrapnel marks in the wall around, which is what you would normally expect to see if it had been a mortar shell or something like that. There were small arms marks in the walls, but it didn't appear to be the normal level of shrapnel that you would associate with a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you told when these houses had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the month when you were taken to these houses and shown them in this state?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think that was quite later on in our tour, well after the halfway point, I think, when I was visiting that particular location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where were these houses depicted in 433/16 from the front-line between Vitez and Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Very close to the front-line, 100, 200 metres. These were houses that were probably in the direct line of fire. So there was bound to be an element of small arms damage as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether these houses were used by the BiH army to direct fire towards Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the case or not, but it was very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were well situated for that purpose; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever in the Hotel Vitez when you heard something or you learned or were told, "That is a Bebe being fired"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You referred to a threat to blow up the SPS or Vitezit factory. Is that a subject you personally discussed with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think I might have been at a meeting where Colonel Blaskic expressed that to Colonel Alastair, but I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You don't remember if it was at a meeting between Blaskic and Duncan or you don't remember whether you were present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I remember the threat, or Darko Gelic mentioned it to me on several occasions, so I'm fully aware that that was said to us on several occasions. My memory fails me, but I could have quite easily been at a meeting, and Colonel Blaskic could have mentioned that to Colonel Alastair or not. I don't know. I remember Colonel Blaskic mentioning it to Colonel Alastair on one particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you were present?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm pretty sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic make it clear to Colonel Duncan that advance notice would be given before any destruction of the factory occurred, so that BRITBAT personnel, as well as others in the area, could be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do recall something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was made clear; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I have a memory of something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the factory ever blown up by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that Darko Gelic made some type of threat that if Vitez was attacked the HVO would shell Zenica; do you recall that or is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yeah, something like that was said. I can't remember the specific circumstances, but, yes, that was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the HVO ever shell Zenica during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were several occasions or a couple of occasions, rather, I can recall when Nora was reported as firing by soldiers on central duty or moving up and down the Lasva Valley, and that there were subsequently explosions in the Zenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were any of these investigated?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, did someone attempt to substantiate that HVO artillery had shelled a location in the city of Zenica or was there no attempt to substantiate that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was the same for -- if the BiH shelled the Vitez area, we would express our concern that innocent civilians were, in all likelihood, to be injured. Those protests were usually made by myself or the appropriate liaison officer to whoever in the respective headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it during your tour the army of BH routinely shelled the centre of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Routinely makes it sound like it was a daily/weekly occurrence. It varied, and I wouldn't say one did it more than the other, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of any reports or MILINFOSUMs or other documents that sought to demonstrate that, in fact, on a particular occasion during your tour, the HVO shelled a civilian location in the city of Zenica? Do you know of any such studies, documents, what have you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any. I can't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You spoke of the death of the BRITBAT interpreter Dobrila. After her death, you went to the Hotel Vitez, as I understood your testimony, and you met personally with Colonel Blaskic or not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think I might have done it on that occasion. I think I might have insisted, under the circumstances, that I speak directly to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And he met with you and he expressed sympathy and regret towards her death; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he promise to assign individuals to an investigative team who would investigate the matter?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he, in fact, assign those investigative resources to a team for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I think there was a local -- there was an HVO representative from Mario Cerkez's brigade and then two other officials that were provided by the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you participated with this team as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, indeed, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And for approximately three or four days, the team conducted an investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that a full-time endeavour during those three or four days?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It took a large percentage of the day on those days, yes, it did. It involved myself, also going to 325 Brigade headquarters, to the Muslim area, because obviously they had been involved in the small arms exchange, so I was trying to get their account of the incident and press them to launch their own investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, was Dobrila killed as a result of a single shot or as a result of a larger, either, spray of gun fire in one direction or of an exchange of gun fire between different locations; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was a small arms exchange on that particular day that started, if I remember correctly, half an hour, an hour early, which was intimated single rounds exchanged between the two sides. Immediately prior to Dobrila's death, there had been an increase in the amount of firing. There were one or two bursts, but for the most part, there was still deliberate single shots. At the time when the round hit Dobrila, there were maybe three or four single shots fired in the area of the captain's house, some of which struck the wall and the ground around on which, unfortunately, killed Dobrila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, from where were the army of BH -- strike that. Where were the army of BH firing positions with respect to this exchange of small arms fire you have described?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were on the high ground to the left of the end of the house where Dobrila stood when the rounds fell into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say the BiH army was firing from the houses across the street from Dobrila's house as you start up the hill, which is the Grbavica feature? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think this explanation would be better served with a large-scale map or a drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Such as the map to your left, yes?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: May I use a piece of paper underneath instead?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You would like to draw on a plain sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. If the registrar could provide the witness with a pen, we will remove the aerial photo, and he can demonstrate his testimony, if the court please. No, no, I think --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: If you flip the photograph over, I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The witness will simply draw on plain paper, if we can provide him with a dark marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you would like to go over there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to warn you that if you speak from your current location, the microphones will not pick you up, so if you could, perhaps, return to the microphone when you have oral testimony to give.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The drawing of the house on the top actually represents this end of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indicating the end of the diagonally-shaped building below the top house which appears to have a door or a front marked on the right-hand side of that diagram; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were two balconies, a lower balcony and the upper balcony. Myself and another captain resided in the top balcony, and Dobrila and her fiancee resided in the bottom floor. Myself, Dobrila and her boyfriend were having a conversation early on in the day when initially the small arms fire broke out. At that point, I left and went upstairs into my room. Dobrila and her boyfriend were still downstairs at the time, and as I came out onto the top balcony, several rounds hit the side of those building, and one of the rounds was the one that went through Dobrila's head and killed her.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As you came out of the balcony on the top of this building, which is the side of the building facing the right hand of the diagram; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Rounds were impacting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Roughly how many rounds hit the building at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you were not injured, I take it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But one of those same rounds hit Dobrila where, in the doorway or through a window or was she outside at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: She stood just inside the house selected by the doorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you explain where this house stood in relation to the exchange of fire between the two firing points, the HVO and BH firing points, to the extent you knew where they were during the earlier exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: These houses on this side of the road belonged to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indicating the bottom of the diagram; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct. And there were a series of trenches immediately adjacent to the road on that side. This side, there were several houses that belonged to the Muslim community, but served the camp --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: -- served the camp area. That was one of the houses that we actually lived in. It was rented from the Muslim family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where is the Grbavica feature in relation to this diagram; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The high point buildings that you saw yesterday on the photographs, on the Grbavica feature that were manned by the BiH as represented by that house marked with BiH there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What's the rough distance from the HVO houses below up to the BiH location you've indicated in the upper right-hand of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know and what's the distance -- the real question would be, degrees, but how many degrees separate the BH military installation that you've indicated in the upper right-hand of the diagram, and the front of the house where you and Dobrila were?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: You mean that angle?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That angle, in other words, a pyramid -- in other words, the variance of degrees from the -- well, I was thinking from the vantage point if someone was down in the HVO trench firing at the BH position, what is that? That variance of degrees, is that 5 degrees, 10 degrees?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would say about 25 to 30 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there other BH positions as you go on up the hill on Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not that would have been able to engage these houses here. That's why these houses are of such the -- they were the ones that had been --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You need to return to the microphone and repeat that, if you could.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To explain. Those were the only houses that had a view over the area and that is why they were of such strategic importance during the attack in Grbavica. The other houses in Grbavica did not have a view over those particular HVO positions or those Croat houses. This was the house or two houses, rather, that were regularly occupied by BiH and that they sniped from those houses onto the Croat/HVO positions adjacent to camp on that side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you completed your use of this plain paper diagram?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Other than to say that the scale is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's not true to scale, in other words?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. If Exhibit 172 could be returned to the easel, that is the aerial photograph, and perhaps we can just find a couple of these locations on the aerial photo so we do have a more accurate sense of the scale. While that is being done --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be D155.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While that is being done, did you visit with this investigative team, the area of the trenches and the HVO structures, to the bottom of Exhibit D155, which you have drawn?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, indeed. I visited the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What did you find there? Did you find any evidence of value, evidence of potential forensic use, spent shell casings or the like?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were spent shell casings there, but bearing in mind the regularity with which there were small arms fire, that wasn't conclusive enough to say that it had come from that particular location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there individual soldiers at those locations in these houses?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: At that particular time, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There was no one there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was no one there. The activity in the area had considerably -- had calmed down in the three or four days afterwards. I had been around to all the local HVO, BiH positions, and obviously it was quite an upset to all the liaison officers and staff that had happened, and I think that message was quite clearly put across to both sides and both communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you visit the BiH army firing point on Exhibit D155?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I couldn't get up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say you couldn't get up there, does that mean it wasn't safe so you weren't able to go up there and perhaps try and interview individuals there? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I had already actually been up to that point on a previous occasion and new that it afforded the type of view for the area. I tried to get up there and I didn't get a lot of cooperation from the local BiH commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, if I could just approach for a moment, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleagues for a moment. I wanted to consult with my colleagues about a specific point of the amount of time given both to the Defence and to the Prosecution. This is the first time, as far as we remember, that the cross-examination has lasted longer than the examination-in-chief, which is causing somewhat of a problem. There are no specific rules in this matter, it's up to the Judges to decide, but we consider it important to make this comment to Mr. Hayman to say that we had started quite awhile ago and that this cross-examination is longer than the examination-in-chief. You said yesterday that you would take the time today to do your cross-examination, but you have had a lot of time already. We have to think of where we're going with this and when we are going to get to the end, Mr. Hayman, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think your comments are well taken. I have, I would say, less than 45 minutes of material left. I think I have taken about the same as the direct so far, which is unusual in this case. Certainly, in the last nine or ten months, our cross-examinations generally have been much shorter than the directs, and the difficulty, with all candour, with this witness, is a lot of opinions on a lot of different subjects, and to dig into those opinions, quite frankly, at least in my judicial system, it is normal for that kind of testimony that the cross-examination take longer than the direct. Obviously we want to avoid that and we will continue to try and avoid that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps you could try to be completed by 3.30 in respect of the reference to your own legal system, we all have references to our legal systems. Perhaps it would be best to try not to refer to it too much. We are attempting to maintain a balance. Yesterday you were concerned about the possibility of being able to conduct a cross-examination. I know that the Judges took that into consideration. We are going to ask that you be finished by 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, of course, up to now, you have already taken three hours in the morning and an hour now, an hour and a half, and it's four hours, and we enjoy listening to you so don't worry. The problem is the following. This time is counted on the other parties. The same thing might happen to you and then it will be counted as hours which will be discounted from your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the court wishes to have a rule that would be any time in excess of the time on direct spent on cross be assessed against the other side, so be it. I don't think we would object to that. I think, in fact, that's been very rare during the Prosecutor's case, and I would expect, I would hope, it would be very rare during the Defence case, but I appreciate Your Honours' comment that I am not grating on Your Honours. I certainly hope not to and I do hope to conclude with this witness reasonably soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will then agree that you will finish by 3.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will do my very best, Your Honour. I would note, though, that the Defence gave up 30 days of testimony vis-à-vis the Prosecutor when the Defence asked for a limit on the parties. They have 90 days -- they had more than 90 and we agreed to take only 60. We, I think, have been a force in trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman. Mr. Hayman. Everybody is going to demonstrate great efforts, including the Judges. We will agree that your objective is to finish by 3.30. Obviously, if you can't, we will take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you Your Honours.
