Counsel, this is the first opportunity I have had in some time to continue with my examination, and I would like to -- I think it would be helpful and we had a transparency with this exhibit sometime in the past, and I believe with Major Bower. If that can be retrieved, perhaps with a different coloured pen, we can utilise that overhead because, quite frankly, I think it would be helpful to know where these three houses are, or three areas, on a map that is to scale. If we can do that quickly, if we can find that overhead, I would propose to do that. Can the registrar assist in that regard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In order to conclude with the previous question, in order to be rigorous but equitable, be assured, Mr. Hayman, that the examination-in-chief lasted 175 minutes, and at five after three, you're at 170. Therefore we're going to ask that you try to be complete by 3.30. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D142.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will approach with the court's leave to assist in placing this on Exhibit 172.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major Bower, I'm going to -- excuse me. Mr. Whitworth, let's find some coloured pens that don't duplicate the colours used by the prior witness. I see there's a green one. Can you approach the Exhibit D142, which is on top of Exhibit 172, and indicate the location of the three areas you previously identified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me simply point out to you that the quality among Judges is not absolutely ensured because we can say that Judge Jorda and Judge Riad are seeing the reflections of the transparency and Judge Shahabuddeen can hardly see it at all. But I don't think you can do any better than that. We have Judge Shahabuddeen who can see now. He will have to have eyes for us then. Thank you. Now I think nobody can see. Well, everyone is equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For the record, let me ask you, sir, if you've indicated on this map in red --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Number 1 is the house where Dobrila was shot and killed, known as the captain's house where I was located. 2 is the line of houses on the south side of the road, which is occupied by the HVO and is occupied by Croatian population and 3 is the two key houses that were circled in Grbavica, occupied by the BiH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One more question on this subject. During the exchange of small arms fire that you noted, do you know from what or which of the houses or locations along the line that is number 2 specific fire came from or did the fire come from that general area represented by number 2 on Exhibit D142?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It came from -- it was coming from the area at the top of the line marked 2, which I have actually coloured in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Which you have coloured in now with a different colour?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was also coming from the BiH positions in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you done with this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After the investigative team --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After the investigative team, of which you were a part, carried out its activity over these three or four days, were there any leads or further investigation that you felt had not been conducted?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, we had done the best we could in questioning the people we found in and around the areas on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you suggest any other investigation or follow-up investigative activity to Colonel Blaskic or his representative on the team?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, at the time, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you concerning the death of Boris, the UNHCR driver.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can I just point out at this stage, Your Honour, that the investigation I conducted was also conducted by the British military police at the same time. All the ballistics evidence, the round's journey that had gone through the building and subsequently through Dobrila and behind her, led us conclusively, to believe, that the round had come from one particular window in one of the HVO side of the road. That was almost irrefutable based on the journey that the round had taken. Despite that, the HVO offered another conclusion that it was a BiH soldier that had crept over from the other side, fired the round from HVO territory and gone back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the BRITBAT military police prepare a report or other documentation concerning their analysis of the trajectory of the bullet?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Exactly the same conclusions were reached by the military police officer who came up and based himself at BRITBAT for that particular location, and I believe he did produce a report to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that report shared with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't recall, I'm afraid. I gave my account to Darko Gelic after the HVO investigative team had given me their account of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it at the end of the day, there was no further investigation, no persons who had not been interviewed, et cetera, that you or Colonel Duncan asked Colonel Blaskic to see was done; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In light of the ballistics evidence, it was quite clear to us that the round had come from one of the HVO positions, and what we were after was, firstly, for Colonel Blaskic to acknowledge the possibility that that was the case, and to do his own investigation to identify who was responsible and punish them accordingly. As far as we were aware, that's not what had taken place. There was a complete denial that the HVO had had anything to do with it, despite overwhelming evidence, as far as we were concerned, to the contrary. And nothing other than the investigative teams conclusion took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the investigative team interview HVO soldiers who were involved on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not to our knowledge. There was nobody there at the time, and I remember speaking to the local battalion commander who dismissed it as of no importance, as far as he was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the local battalion commander was not cooperative?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: (Nod).

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that reported to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't remember, to be honest, at the time. It was -- no, I can't remember. I wouldn't like to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let's turn, since time is slipping by, let's move on to the death of the UNHCR driver on the 14th of August, 1993. I believe you said again, an investigation was carried out that spanned two days' time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who participated in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was the only one that took part in the investigation, who was able to visit both locations, the alleged firing point and the impact point where Boris had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Nonetheless, did the HVO assign someone to work with you on the investigation?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I believe they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many people was that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think there was just one on that particular occasion, but there could have been more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But that person, I take it, was not allowed by Commander Djidic to go to the scene of the destination of the bullet to participate with you in that aspect of the investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes. Early on in our tour, Commander Sefkija had been quite willing to let HVO or Croat representatives into Stari Vitez in an attempt to re-establish electricity, telephone cables, but subsequent to that, in his opinion, what had happened was they had been spying on the BiH defensive arrangements within Stari Vitez, and so he stopped. He refused from that point onwards to allow any representative, and it happened to affect the outcome of the inquiry of Boris's death.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What did you find at the suspected firing point, which, I believe, is indicated by an orange line from which an arrow emanates on Exhibit 441? What did you find at the suspected firing point? Did you find any evidence, forensic evidence of value?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: None whatsoever, other than knowing that it was a regularly occupied position from which HVO soldiers sniped into the area. The only real reason I have concluded that it came from that point was the direction of the vehicle and its orientation when the round had struck.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the conclusion of this two-day investigation, did you suggest any leads or additional investigative activity that you desired the HVO representative to conduct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I suggested to them that, bearing in mind what I had found, that there was a strong possibility that it had come from that particular sanga (phoen) trench position on the top and asked them to investigate that and expose who was responsible. I don't know how far in their investigation went, but when I asked that, it was met with a blank refusal that any HVO soldier would have actually done that in the first place. So from that, I concluded that there would be no subsequent investigation on their part. They just weren't prepared to entertain the thought that that was a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it before or after this point that you saw the sniper rifle depicted in Exhibits 82-9, 82-10, and 433-19?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think it was after, after I had -- after this event that I saw that sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So as of the time of the investigation, you had not seen any sniper rifle in the theatre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How much later did you see this sniper rifle in the possession of a Vitezovi soldier?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That sniper rifle was identified on my second or third visit to Kraljevic, which will be detailed in the log, so it would be quite easy to look at the dates, but I would have thought maybe three or four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At least a month later; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Well, I said three or four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Three to four weeks after the end of the investigation you saw this rifle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: At the time of the investigation, after discussing the range, the accuracy needed, the calibre of the weapon, myself and the intelligence officer who was pretty well-educated about weapon capabilities, did actually suggest that it would be a weapon like that or something of that nature, responsible for it. Four weeks later, one appeared in Kraljevic's hands. It could quite easily have been construed that that weapon had appeared after the time and was not responsible for Boris's death, but bearing in mind they are quite a rare weapon, and that was the only one we ever saw within the Lasva Valley, we came to what we thought was a pretty safe conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you or a BRITBAT representative ask that the investigation be reopened in light of the identification of this suspect weapon in the possession of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No. The investigation had terminated some time earlier. It was a month later and, again, we were busy engaged in other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are all the photographs I identified, are they all of the same gun?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They are, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During the Convoy of Joy incident, did BRITBAT have occasion to fire on Croats and kill or injure Croats in the course of trying to free or protect the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I simply note that this wasn't part of the direct examination. I have no objection to the question. But it should, of course, go against -- not taken away from the Prosecutor's time on a question that was not part of direct. The substance of it, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's correct. If you want to ask the question, you can, but do it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll use my own time for the balance of this cross-examination, Mr. President, if it pleases the court. If counsel is making a relevance or beyond the scope objection, I beg to differ, as there was testimony about the Convoy of Joy, the behaviour of crowds, and the fact is, although I'm not suggesting it was inappropriate, BRITBAT fired upon and killed a number of HVO and/or Croat civilians in connection with the Convoy of Joy incident. That is relevant information vis-à-vis the behaviour of these crowds and what was going on in the Vitez enclave at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Hayman, you will allow the presiding Judge to have his opinion on this issue. It is true that the cross-examination must not move away too far from the direct examination. It's true that this fact was not included in the direct examination. I hope that I'm not giving you this as new information. I'm sure you know this already, but we're trying to gain some time here. If you tell us that it's particularly important for you, then ask the question. I just want to recall to you that it was not part of the direct examination because the Judges do listen now and again, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I won't take that bait, Your Honour. Of course the court studies the evidence and I wouldn't suggest or hint otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you answer the question briefly? If not, I will move on?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did BRITBAT have occasion to fire on Croat civilians or soldiers in connection with the Convoy of Joy incident?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I bore -- I did not bear witness to that. It was reported as happening, and there were numerous instances throughout our tour when both Muslims, Croats, HVO and BiH were fired upon with restraint by our soldiers in order to secure U.N. personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now we come to the last subject of my cross-examination, and that is the conflict and attack on the Grbavica feature of the 7th and 8th of September, 1993. You've indicated on Defence Exhibit 142, in red, the BiH army firing point in connection with this earlier exchange. Was that structure or in that area, was there, in fact, a BiH army battalion headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. If that was the case, it was a pretty fool hearted place to put one, bearing in mind, its prominence on the hillside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever visit any of the BiH army facilities and locations in that area, that is, at the foot along the road of the Grbavica feature?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The houses in the Muslim community in Grbavica didn't seem to have any central military location, other than those two derelict houses which were used as lookout positions and usually constantly occupied by one or two BiH soldiers. But there was not a headquarters, battalion or otherwise, in the Grbavica, to the best of my knowledge, other than being the house where the local militia commander lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Am I correct that the house you identified on Defence Exhibit 142 as being a BiH army location is within 500 metres of the perimeter of the BRITBAT base?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, it's probably about 400, 500 metres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that a subject about which Colonel Blaskic was continually protesting to UNPROFOR, that the BiH army was firing on HVO positions from within the 500 metre radius of the base, which UNPROFOR had proclaimed a fire-free zone?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Colonel Blaskic did complain. Likewise, the HVO positions adjacent to the camp reciprocated and it was my job on numerous locations to visit the local Grbavica commander and the commander at 325 Brigade to protest about the regularity of small arms exchanges within the camp area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Prior to the assault on Grbavica on 7 and 8 September, 1993, how many civilian sniper victims were there from the BiH army snipers on Grbavica during your tour?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to guess. I would say probably a dozen or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that during the attack, the HVO made no attempt to encircle the rear of the Grbavica feature so as to ensure an evacuation route for any civilians, as well as the BiH army on the feature?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I concur with that, but from a military point of view, it would have been foolish any way, because the area marked is BiH territory, and no military commander worth his salt would send troops in and try and attack around form the back for fear of running into other forces deployed over the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In fact, this is the route that was used to evacuate civilians from Grbavica; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: After they evacuated on the night of the 7th, how many BiH army soldiers remained in Grbavica; do you know or are you not able to tell because they were in houses, structures, trenches, and fortifications?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The latter is true?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We estimated it may be 10 to a dozen, bearing in mind the amount of small arms fire taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But the fact is you couldn't tell because they were hiding themselves?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The infantry attack began on the morning of the 8th; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, the BBC film we watched yesterday, Exhibit 443, stated that the BiH army withdrawal was at approximately 13.00 hours or 1.00. Is that correct? Is that, in fact, when the BiH army forces appeared to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. That's a BBC detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When do you think they withdrew or do you know?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Certainly from what I observed as I drove along the road, while the fighting was still going on, I saw very few people as the HVO were clearing through the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On the 8th, how much of the battle did you observe or to what extent were you doing other things?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: For the morning of the 8th, I spent in the offices mess with a fair of binoculars, taking photographs as the HVO troops went up to point 3 on the map, which was their launch point for the assault. And then around lunchtime, I drove through in an armoured vehicle, observed troops crossing the road, small arms exchanges taking place. I went down to the Hotel Vitez to speak to Colonel Blaskic, but spoke to Darko Gelic. Colonel Blaskic was unavailable at the time. I stayed down there for half an hour and then drove back up in the afternoon, after lunch sometime. I can't remember when it was. That's when I took the photographs showing the extent to which the buildings were burning as I returned up. That must have been afternoon, early afternoon, afternoon time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you were gone from the BRITBAT base from roughly when to when, on the 8th of September?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to say. I was maybe gone for a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you say when you thought the soldiers withdrew or simply that they had withdrawn by the time you returned from your trip to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We assumed that they had withdrawn. As I drove down to Hotel Vitez, for the first time, I saw very little activity but could hear small arms exchanges taking place. From that I assumed that there were still soldiers left in Grbavica, but on my return back an hour or two hours later, the HVO soldiers were walking around, crossing the road and were making moves to continue up the hill. By the afternoon period on my return, they had effectively been through the village, and I assumed whatever BiH were present were now dead, captured, or had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The BBC broadcast said that the flag was raised on Grbavica at teatime. In the language of your nation, when is teatime?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That would fit in with the time I've just given, I would say about 4.00, 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: 1600 or 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that accurate, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It fits in with my recollection of timings of events on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The BBC tape then says that looting and burning occurred later on in the night time. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I think as I said yesterday, there were numerous vehicles and lorries turned up. Once it had been declared clear, I presume, the word very quickly went out and people turned up to salvage and loot whatever they could before the place completely went up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The scavengers arrived in buses and trucks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No. People turned up with horse-drawn trailers. Some people turned up in trucks. People were pushing sofas down the road, or whatever it is that they could get their hands on, naturally, trying to salvage anything worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many houses were burning then when you came back in the afternoon, at mid afternoon?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Quite a few. I would have said about half of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Half of the total that you saw burning on the 8th or half of all the houses on Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I would have said a good half of the houses. It certainly presented a great wall of smoke that looked as if there was a fair number. As I drove through and took photographs, I would say that half the houses were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many more were burned after the one's that were burning in the middle of the afternoon on the 8th? On the 8th, that is, say, that night?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would say two or three days later when I went back in, most of them had been burned, and everything had been stripped from the place. People were even coming in and prying the wood out of the window sills that they could probably then use for timber wood. I'm not sure. But all the buildings were stripped of whatever useful things were in them, and well over half, probably three-quarters of them had been burned. At that stage, I can't recall the state of the mosque, but it seemed reasonably intact on the 8th but could quite well have been on fire at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see individuals lighting houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that the civilians and the scavengers who came after the battle was over, were just as capable of lighting houses on fire as were any soldiers who may have been lingering in the area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can't think what their motive would be to light the fires, considering they were trying to salvage whatever they could from the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: These were local people, at least, in part, weren't they, who were descending on the hill, -- who were coming to the location after the battle was over and stripping the wood off the windows and so forth?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I presume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: These were the same people that these sniper victims had been their families, their friends and so forth; correct? Weren't these people? Did you see the people on the BBC tape yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman. Ask questions, please. Don't make suggestions and then using your own suggestions, you come to questions. Go to the question directly. Don't make suggestions. Don't make any comments, please. You're pulling the witness into your own suggestions. Try to ask your questions directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see whether the locals who descended on Grbavica, on the 8th, to loot, et cetera, what was their state or could you tell?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They just seemed to be coming down scavenging and looting for whatever there could be. They were people from as far up the valley as Nova Bila, Novi Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Zuti come with a group of men to loot and scavenge?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing Zuti.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Zuti was from Nova Bila; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Nova Bila, Novi Travnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How do you recall that people came from Nova Bila, specifically, if you didn't see Zuti or some indication of Zuti's men?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There were a lot of people in Nova Bila than there are Zuti and there were numerous flatbed trucks and I knew a lot of people in Nova Bila whom I dealt with when doing the evacuations and could identify items and trucks that I had seen in the vicinity during the lotting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you participate in evacuating any persons from Grbavica on the 7th or 8th?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The man in the black uniform, Exhibit 444, if that could be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Let me remind you to speak a little bit more slowly so that it can all be properly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Turning to Exhibit 444, the individual on the far left; is there anything about that individual that leads you to believe he was a member of the unit the Jokers, other than the fact his dress is black?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir. Yesterday, I said that he was dressed typically in the fashion I had seen the Jokeri, but my driver and signaller who worked with me throughout the tour said they had identified an insignia on one or two of the gentlemen present near the Grbavica area. They also recognised the Jokeri insignia that was shown to demonstrate, as far as I was concerned, the type of dress that the Jokeri wore. I didn't say that was a member of the Jokeri, but the faces and the insignia worn by one or two members present at Grbavica were identified as being Jokeri.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say faces, what do you mean you identified a face?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A couple of faces that I identified were, as far as I was concerned, people that I had met previously who sat on the balcony at the Swiss cottage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you got close enough to identify their faces, did you see any insignia or markings on them that would have identified them as Jokers, had they been wearing any such insignia?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not. For the most part, there are very few insignia, actually. Usually the specialists army units wear with pride their insignia. None of the soldiers you will see on the film have got much insignia on. Some of them have "Vojne Policije" on which intimates that they might be from the military police. You can't go entirely on what people wear, nor can you specifically identify units on the whole that are present. All I said yesterday was that I had identified Turtko soldiers and chaps wearing Jokeri dress and we had also identified people with that insignia at Grbavica during the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said somebody else had but not you?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I identified faces, chaps wearing the black uniform, and it was confirmed. One of my soldiers, who was with me in the vehicle, said, "Oh, sir, I have seen one of the guys with the clowns hat on his arm," to me indicating that he had also seen evidence that there were Jokeri present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When was that, was this after the fight or during the fight?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This was at the end of the battle, at the end of the day when these soldiers were work walking around and the battle ceased and the flag had been put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the end of the 8th?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions. Did you go back to the Hotel Vitez then or did you only go to the Hotel Vitez once on the 8th?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I can only remember going down when the battle was taking place, but it's likely that I went down again. I would sometimes go three or four times a day, depending on what the circumstances were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you went and you saw Darko Gelic and you said there are houses burning, what's going on at Grbavica, or words to that effect; what did he say to you, that there's no military operation going on?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: His reply was a blank refusal that there was any military operation going on and when I asked to speak to Colonel Blaskic or any of the staff officers, he said none of them are present and available to speak to you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this at noon or at six p.m.?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you go more slowly, please? It's not because you have gone for three-quarters of an hour that you should pretend that you are going faster by torturing the interpreters. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm guilty of two sins, Mr. President. I'm almost done. I appreciate the court's patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please complete quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When did you have this conversation? Was this at noon or around the lunch hour?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: This was a conversation I went down to Hotel Vitez on the lunch time, early afternoon, of the 8th during which you pointed out I was absent from the Grbavica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the BiH had not yet withdrawn from Grbavica as of noontime; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, if you remember, I said that as I was going through, there were small arms exchange. I couldn't see any army or soldiers and left down to Hotel Vitez to return an hour, two hours later, by which time all the HVO soldiers were walking around on the road going through the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was any other protest or expression of concern made, other than your, noon on the 8th visit, to the Hotel Vitez, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was no point, as far as I was concerned. The battle was over and done. The HVO had claimed Grbavica and the Muslim population had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the answer is "no"?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. Thank you, Your Honours, and Mr. President for your patience. I have concluded. I would offer, I think, 444 is already in on behalf of the Prosecution. If Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Perhaps you are looking for D155.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The transparency?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's also the transparency which is D142.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: D142, Your Honour, I believe is probably already in evidence. To the extent I need to re-offer it because there are new markings on it, I would re-offer it. May I inquire of the registrar, D155 is what?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's the drawing that the witness made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the paper drawing. I would offer D155, and I have concluded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Since this hearing has been conducted the way it has been conducted, we will take a 20-minute break, then the Prosecutor will ask any questions he wishes to ask and then the Judges will ask theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you now have the redirect, but stay within the scope of the cross-examination. I hope it will not be too long, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Captain.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a follow-up on several questions asked by Defence counsel on cross. Bear with me if I, again, jump from topic to topic. You said in response to questions by Defence counsel that Blaskic was an informed commander?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that Defence counsel raised the subject of Vares, him being informed of what was happening in Vares; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about Zepce? Did you ever receive information during your tour about what was happening up in Zepce. When I say "received information," I mean received that information from HVO or HVO personnel?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, indeed, sir. On numerous occasions, I received updates from Darko Gelic, Colonel Blaskic's liaison officer, on activity taking place in the Zepce, Vares and Kiseljak areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, you were in the armed forces for some time, and it's quite normal, is it not, for a commander, such as then Colonel Blaskic, to be well-informed about what is happening in the area of his responsibility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Absolutely true, sir, yes. It's important to get communication from wherever to execute strategic command like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In your opinion, based on what information you got, Blaskic and his personnel were well-informed?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Very well-informed, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, he also had quite a few number of soldiers under his command, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He did. He had several brigades in the Lasva Valley that we were aware of. From the point of view of being informed about what was happening everywhere, we assumed also that he was making policy/strategic decisions about what was happening in other HVO Croat pockets like Vares and Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can ask you one more time, when you're answering the question, just look at the Judges. That would be a little better. You mentioned this chap "Zuti" during both direct and cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you talked about Darko Kraljevic and the Vitezovi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many Vitezovi were there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We estimated, or I estimated, rather, there to be 20 or 30 of them. And Zuti was -- I don't know. I have no reference to figures, but I should imagine there was a small gang of them that, when they weren't soldiers or whatever, were part of his entourage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about the Jokeri? Approximately how many of them?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As a military police platoon, a normal size would be about 30 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If any of those units were doing anything outside or contrary to what Blaskic wanted, did Blaskic have the military manpower to take them out?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. He quite easily had sufficient manpower, weapons, whatever you want, resources to stop them doing whatever they were doing. He also appeared to have the necessary command structure and position himself to be able to execute and discipline them if that was necessary. "Execute" was the wrong word, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, during your tour, starting with the instance on the 11th of June when Blaskic ordered the release of the U.N. vehicles, did Kraljevic and the local HVO obey?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: All HVO forces obeyed eventually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When Gelic went out to retrieve the trucks taken from the Convoy of Joy, when you were with him and they met the local HVO individuals at various locations, did those HVO commanders obey Blaskic's order?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They did, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned on cross-examination Mario Cerkez's distaste in complying with the wishes of Colonel Blaskic. Do you remember those questions on cross?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you highlighted that when you attempted to get aid through, there initially was some resistance from Cerkez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When the final decision came, did Cerkez obey Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He did, indeed, yes, sir. Albeit reluctantly, he did obey, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me change subjects with you, if you will. You mentioned the series of photographs that you took, one of which was shown both by the Defence and the Prosecution of Valenta, Blaskic, Kordic, Kostroman, Santic, Skopljak being taken down to the Kiseljak U.N. facility. Do you remember those photographs?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you also said that was sometime in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could put that back on the ELMO. I'm not sure, for the record, again, Mr. Dubuisson, which 80 that is. I think that's 80/8?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's right. It's 80/8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You - and by "you," I'm talking about UNPROFOR - took quite an entourage of people down there, did you not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We did, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you mentioned in passing on cross that there were two warrior companies to load all these individuals up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were eight or ten warriors, each of which will hold a section of eight men. But in this particular case, it was holding three or four representatives from the HVO/Croat hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned that you took all of them down to the U.N. facility in Kiseljak, and several days later you brought them back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said in cross-examination you didn't bring all of them back?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also said on cross-examination that, shortly thereafter, those people, who you had taken to Kiseljak, made it back into the Vitez area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How did they get back?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I will reiterate what I said earlier, that we had strong suspicions that the helicopter flights coming in and out with considerable regularity were bringing people in and out, senior military and political figures like Dario Kordic, Colonel Blaskic, and the like, but that was supposition on our part. Bearing in mind that we did see them again, it was the only explanation we could offer at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The fact of the matter, Captain, was that these high HVO officials got back to Vitez without the assistance of UNPROFOR; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on that fact, do you believe that it would have been just as easy for Colonel Blaskic to make that trip as well?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In either direction, yes, sir, that's correct. That's one of the ways we assumed he was executing command in other areas outside the Lasva pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can turn from that exhibit to Exhibit 435, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's a map, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Captain, you noted in your direct and in cross that the green circled area was the general area where these individuals were held, but right close to the front line; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was a couple hundred metres from the front-line, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe there were how many displaced Bosnian Muslims in there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I counted five or six families. There was about 20 to 30 people all told, about ten to a dozen of which were children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You found out about these people, did you not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How far were these people being held from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: A kilometre, 1.400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were being held by Blaskic's men, were they not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were being held, sir, yes, by -- they were stopped from leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Vague as to the term "Blaskic's men." Could we be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were all his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, on cross-examination, Mr. President, we had a specific discussion of who they were, militia, military police. It doesn't clarify the matter for counsel to use vague and, let's be frank, derogatory terms of the type he's using. We should have a clear, specific record in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The objection is sustained. The cross-examination was conducted for clarifications about each of the troops and the militias and the different formations. Try to be a bit more specific, Mr. Kehoe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain Whitworth, these were HVO Vitez brigade soldiers, were they not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: HVO Vitez brigade soldiers knew about the presence of those people a kilometre away from the Hotel Vitez, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As did the elements of the military police as well who stopped us living at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The two units, two separate units, in the HVO knew about the presence of these individuals; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They did, indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Initially, Darko Gelic even informed you that they could not leave; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Based on that, do you have any opinion whether or not Blaskic knew that those displaced people were being held on the front-line area?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I assumed that Darko Gelic, who was acting in the same light as I act on behalf of the Colonel, i.e., with his authority and blessing, and that Colonel Blaskic was aware of the fact that those troops were actually -- those civilians, rather, were detained in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me speak on a couple of subjects, and again we're going to shift subjects. We're going to the Dobrila Kolaba murder. With the assistance of the usher, if we can flip back to that Defence Exhibit, and if I may approach the witness briefly? Let me just flip that plastic. I'm going to use that as well. Can you see this, Captain?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, from the questions by Defence counsel, did you receive some suggestion that Defence counsel tried to indicate a firing point from the BiH position on the top of the Grbavica feature?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They did try to indicate that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked the question -- I think the question and the answer is vague. I asked questions. If there is a comment that the witness doesn't like -- if the witness feels I asked an inappropriate question -- what was the question? Let's hear it. Let's have it on the record. This conversation occurring between counsel and the witness is too elliptical, I think, for the record in this case. If there is some suggestion that I have done something improper, let's have it in the record so we're precise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have got to be clear here, because the interpreter also has to have time to distinguish the question from the answer. It's not that easy for me either. Reformulate your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain, from the questions presented to you by Defence counsel, did you infer some indication by those questions that he suggested that the firing point for the killing of Dobrila was the feature in Grbavica overlooking the BRITBAT base?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No comments, Mr. Kehoe, please. Here I can't agree with you. You haven't asked the witness if he thought that he was asked to suggest that. We have to be fair to all parties here. Keep things a little lighter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were asked questions on cross about the BiH position on the top of the Grbavica feature, were you not?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I was, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned during both direct and cross that the HVO conducted an investigation of the Dobrila killing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they not conclude that the firing point was, in fact, from an HVO trench and that it was never up on a BiH position?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: When I pointed out the trajectory of the round that actually struck Dobrila, they reluctantly conceded that it must have originated from the HVO side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From the HVO's investigation, they concluded that it was not from the BiH position on top of the Grbavica feet; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the firing point that you took them to, as you just mentioned, was an HVO trenching area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was one of the houses occupied by the HVO, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Their conclusion was that an ABiH soldier crawled into that trench?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was not a trench. It was actually the top floor of one of the buildings that were occupied by the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was a house that was in control of the HVO, but that an ABiH soldier somehow surreptitiously got into that house and killed Dobrila from that point?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, went around the back, got up the stairs into the room, shot from the window, and then left the building via the same way, crossed the open road and then re-entered the ABiH territory during the small arms exchange that was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You disagreed with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that you can move on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This has already been dealt with from every side possible. The Trial Chamber is in a position to reach a decision. Move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll move on from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, there were denials on the killing of Boris, the UNHCR driver, in Stari Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those denials on HVO involvement came from Darko Gelic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was the same individual you mentioned on cross-examination that said that no military operation was transpiring in Grbavica that you were witnessing on the 7th and the 8th?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's true, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you found this weapon and after you had done your investigation, you disagreed with the HVO's position on that as well?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I did, indeed, sir, and felt that they could have made considerably more effort to investigate it themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Those are the two murders that you disagreed with and for which no HVO soldier was punished, to your knowledge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it surprise you during your tour and after those experiences that no HVO soldier was punished for the massacre in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, sir. It follows the pattern that we saw of the lack of will and commitment towards the pursuance of seeing the right thing done under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope. I ask to be able to cross-examine this witness about Ahmici, subsequent investigations into Ahmici, orders by our client to investigate Ahmici, because this witness should tell the court, has he been given that information, or is he being misled into giving false and inappropriate testimony to this court by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Move to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk about Stari Vitez. You noted during cross-examination that people were using improvised weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted that women sometimes were defending their houses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: On occasion, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted that Sefkija Djidic told you that there was a cache of ammunition in that location; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He did, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was ICRC and UNHCR routinely supplying the Muslims in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: With medical supplies and food, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about ammunition?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They, like ourselves, went to great lengths to prevent and eliminate that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: We had our own liaison officer based with the UNHCR who oversaw activities like loading and unloading; likewise, we had a liaison officer working with the ICRC whose conduct was impeccable as far as making sure that any casualties and delivery of medical supplies were always aboveboard and as agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How do you know that UNHCR was not routinely taking trucks of supplies loaded with weapons into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: If I was supervising and organising an aid delivery, one of the measures I would take to try and imbue the HVO and the Croats with confidence would be to allow them to choose, out of a convoy of however many vehicles, which particular vehicles that they wanted to take for themselves and which they would allow into Kruscica, so that if weapons would get into -- basically who was packing the vehicles could not guarantee that those weapons would not end up in the hands of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the selection of trucks going to Stari Vitez from the HVO warehouse was random?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: To the best effect, yes, it was as random as it could be. At this point --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I had mentioned the HVO warehouse in my question. I stand corrected; I did say that. The UNHCR warehouse.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would also like to point out that all these supplies originated from Split in Croatian territory and came up through an extensive HVO and Croat area. We experienced no such problems when all those vehicles were transiting through Muslim and BiH territory south of the Lasva Valley. It was treated as unacceptable to stop the UNHCR convoys. Everybody, as far as we were concerned, was aware that all efforts were made to minimise and avoid those types of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please ask the witness to slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We would like to cross-examine this witness about, apparently, his knowledge of the standard operating procedures at the UNHCR warehouse in Zenica, in light of this new testimony beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is clearly not beyond the scope, given the fact that Defence counsel went into it at some length, this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen, let's try to put some order to this. That's my role. First of all, there will not be a cross-cross-examination. We have never operated that way. With my colleagues, we have all agreed that the cross-examination must be adapted to the direct examination, and the redirect to the cross-examination. This is not a mathematical rule. I've already said this on several occasions. We apply it with some degree of flexibility. Second of all, I would ask the witness to limit himself to answers to the questions and not to make comments; otherwise, it is going to degenerate. I understand that the Defence at that point becomes concerned and wants to bring information to the Judges. Last of all, I would like to say - I should have said this first - the interpreters can no longer work under these conditions. Mr. Kehoe, ask a further question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm almost done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: -- but remain within the scope of the cross-examination; otherwise, I am going to set a time limit, beyond which we are going to stop, as we did yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm almost completed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stari Vitez, who was doing the attacking, the HVO or the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was my impression, sir, that the HVO initiated the majority of the exchanges that took place. The circumstances in Stari Vitez were very difficult. They were making every effort to conserve ammunition and would, therefore, resist any temptation to spend unnecessary ammunition. With the Croat/HVO positions, they were in no position to try to make offensive against whatsoever, and that was only to the advantage of the HVO to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were asked on cross-examination whether or not Blaskic allowed civilians to leave Stari Vitez, and you mentioned that you passed that message on on several occasions. I believe that was your response to counsel's questions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Initially, nobody left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to leave, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ultimately, did some people in Stari Vitez leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ultimately, Captain, did some people in Stari Vitez leave?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, we were eventually allowed to remove maybe a dozen or so people who were old or injured or required regular medical attention that they couldn't get within the limited confines of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After that, did civilians continue to remain in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After these people had left?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These people in Stari Vitez, can you see the burning of the village of Kruscica from there? Excuse me, the burning of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope, absolutely beyond the scope. As one can see, in Grbavica or Zenica -- I know what counsel is trying to do. It is very clear. I can tell the court if it wants more. Absolutely beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I respond? The response is this: Counsel has suggested to this court that these people were free to walk out of there. And what these people concluded, based on what they saw around them, is that if they left, their village would have been destroyed, burnt, and looted, just like every other village in the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's a valid answer. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you see Grbavica from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: You could, indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you see the village of Donji Vecerska and Gacice?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They were close enough to be able to see what went on there in terms of when buildings were burned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the people in Stari Vitez know what had happened in villages like Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: They knew, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why didn't these civilians leave?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was their opinion that if they left, it would be literally handing over their homes and the rest of the Lasva Valley to the Croats and that there would be no future for their families. As far as they were concerned, they were quite prepared to stand and defend their homes, regardless of what it took. It was that simple and clear-cut, as far as they were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have a moment, Mr. President. I have nothing further, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Captain Whitworth, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to ask you for some clarifications, and if you are in a position to give them to me without entering into too many details, we have heard enough details. I will go quickly through parts of your testimony. You mentioned that Colonel Blaskic was well-informed in the area and had a good understanding of the situation. These are almost your words.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Of course, you are a military man. Of course, you know better than me - I'm not a military man - what a commander should be aware of. Did you build this assessment on your military knowledge or also on concrete indications that he was well-informed and, as you said, had a good understanding of the whole area? You had concrete indications?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Sir, that conclusion was really -- we came to that at the end of our tour, after all of us, the Colonel and the liaison officers, had made observations throughout the tour. I personally witnesses and bore messages from Hotel Vitez to Colonel Alastair detailing the situation in other parts of the area. I had witnessed different types of communication equipment, which we weren't aware that they had. Our overall impression was that he was an effective commander at a strategic level because he was well-informed about the areas which were supposedly under his command in Third OP zone. This was an opinion we came to at the end. It wasn't one we jumped to, and there was information from several sources that led us to that final conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: On the ground, not academic.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned, as you have repeated now, that he had an effective command and control over his soldiers on the ground, including military police. Those were your words. You ruled out some kind of conversation which apparently happened with Colonel Duncan where he was considered as a puppet commander ignored by the locals.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he was not a puppet commander?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: As far as we were concerned, that wasn't the case. If we wanted something done, then it would be Colonel Blaskic we petitioned to achieve that. Ultimately, although it might take time to disseminate the information and his orders, eventually it would happen in one form or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Being an effective commander and having control over his soldiers on the ground, would you rule out the fact that certain major incidents, like the burning of villages and so on, could happen in spite of his orders or without his knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I would say, sir, that circumstances are very difficult - command and control is always very difficult in battle - and that I could anticipate circumstances arising where soldiers would be in a high state of adrenaline or excitement, that things like that could happen. Certainly, to me, it appeared that it was systematic, bearing in mind the number of houses that were actually burned during this type of attack. If it was a smaller number, then I would have been prepared to accept that, but the fact that we're talking virtually all the buildings in a place like Grbavica are levelled to the ground because they were Muslim-occupied and not Croat-occupied, it suggests strongly to me that it's a policy, rather than something taking place at the spur of the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You just mentioned Grbavica. You showed us a video, I think, where houses have been burning, and a soldier was walking around with a butcher's hatchet in his hand.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that you found somebody with his head chopped off.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is the carrying of a hatchet a weapon used in the army now at the end of the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to make the connection. It is not a weapon, sir. My conclusion from that was not that that particular weapon had been responsible for the decapitation, but it looked to me, when I took the photograph, that it was simply a trophy that had been acquired from one of the Muslim homes during the looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there any investigation undertaken?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, there wasn't, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Neither about the destruction nor the killing?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The bodies that were found were identified as wearing Armija uniforms and so were soldiers. I personally did not witness it. I was told that the head of the decapitated soldier appeared in a bag down in Busovaca but that was hearsay. I don't know who that came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned that Colonel Blaskic was always up and down the Lasva Valley, and he had an active role. How much could he travel without the UNPROFOR assistance?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The assumption that he was active came from the fact that it was very difficult to identify his whereabouts at times and it was repeatedly told to me that he was not in the Hotel Vitez. On occasion, I did bump into him once or twice in the Nova Bila area, so he obviously was taking an active role in that way. He spent, if what Darko Gelic's liaison officer tells me is correct, he spent a considerable amount of time out of the Hotel Vitez itself. His movements within the Lasva Valley were limited because of the movement of the BiH territory, obviously, which was as far as Travnik area, Novi Travnik, and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: His travelling up and down, would it be possible to places like Ahmici or Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, very easily, sir, they are on the main road. They are literally a mile, a few kilometres away from the Hotel Vitez and they are all on the edge of the HVO territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke of the trenches, you said they were well situated to prevent the Armija and they were done to the knowledge of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, sir, I said they were obviously well planned by a professional officer. There were several members of the JNA, ex-members of the JNA, in the HVO based in the hotel. And the fact that these trenches were well-positioned and cited was what limited the Armija's ability to penetrate and gain ground in the Lasva Valley area, so far as we were concerned, the defence was laid out and well planned, not by some local militia commander but by, obviously, by a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The fact how these trenches are being built and by whom, by prisoner civilians, would that also be the domain of these JNA or would it be the commander's --

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The actual digging of the trenches would be the local militia on the ground. I saw no evidence of civilians or prisoners digging trenches. The trenches were -- well, let's say usually established during the night. There was digging -- trenches would appear the following day or changes to them would appear. So there weren't prisoners involved in digging them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke of Anto Valenta as a senior political figure and the policy maker in the Lasva Valley, and Colonel Blaskic as the key military figure?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We know what the policy maker is supposed to do and what the military, let's say, commander is doing. But would you consider the military commander as executing the policy?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The executor of the policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The executor of the policy?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's how we interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: While executing this policy, could it be done in a way avoiding destruction or the destruction that happened, the burning and all this that we've listened to?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, it could, sir, yes. There's no reason whatsoever for the systematic clearance and destruction like that, once the area has been cleared of troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that in Stari Vitez, I think there was a decision of the HVO, that in case of invasion by the BiH, they would explode the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How much would this endanger the civilians?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: The ammunition factory was a kilometre outside of the Vitez town centre, but our own assessment of the damage that would be created, which was done by our explosives and engineer experts said that there would be a lot of damage from shrapnel and bits of buildings and the like. It would create quite a hole, but most of the damage would be done by the debris that would fly away from the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain.

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen? Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Captain, I apologise in advance if I should appear to be raising matters which you have already covered. The fault, in that case, would be mine in that I would not have been paying as much attention as I should have been doing. I want to talk about the hospital at Nova Bila. There was a hospital there?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the patients in that hospital, were they exclusively Croats or exclusively Muslims or a bit of one and a bit of the other?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Can I first explain, sir, that it wasn't actually a hospital, it was a catholic church that had been converted into a hospital, and that was the only real medical facility that the HVO and the Croat people had in the Lasva pocket. So circumstances were very difficult for them in that respect. As far as I witnessed, the only people that were in there were Croats, although on one occasion, there were some Muslim gypsies residing in Vitez town centre who were injured during shell fall, and they were hospitalised in that hospital. So that was the only occasion I saw Muslims in there. They were just local gypsies that drifted around the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic gave certain instructions about evacuation?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: In what respect, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Of the patients in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He expressed a wish on several occasions that people should be evacuated from the hospital because the hospital was stretched in terms of the numbers it was expected to deal with and the facilities that it could offer. For example, during the fall of Travnik, there was a large influx of casualties, most of which were suffering from shrapnel or gunshot wounds, and so there were requests at that time from the hospital staff for us to organise an evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding you to mean that his instructions presented no distinction between Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: There was no such distinction, sir, no, but the people in the hospital were Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, tell me about Mr. Anto Valenta and Mayor Santic. I gathered from what you said that Mr. Valenta favoured separation, a policy of separation, whereas, Mayor Santic was prepared to accept a certain degree of integration. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That was the impression I was given by both those gentlemen, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: From what you saw happening on the ground, whose policies would you say were, in fact, being implemented?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Those were the ones of Anto Valenta, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would that have been apparent to any objective onlooker?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I think at the end of our six-month tour, when you study each of the incidents that took place, that would be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say from all the information you had that that would or would not have been clear to General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: He's a professional soldier with, as I always interpreted it, a good understanding of what is happening in his area of responsibility, so I can't see why he would not see that as happening around him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
