utterances.text: I want to talk to you a little about Vitez and Stari Vitez. The impression I have from what you said was the balance of military assault favoured Vitez against Stari Vitez. Most of the shooting was coming from Vitez and directed to Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, whilst I can't say I stood in no-man's land and counted off who started first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand that. Now, was it your impression that the prospect of killing civilians in Stari Vitez at any time operated to restrain the use of military force from Vitez directed against Stari Vitez? That's a difficult question, Captain?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I'm just reflecting and thinking about the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Were civilians killed in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: If I was to be honest, sir, I would say that my overall impression that no consideration was given to the civilians within Stari Vitez, and that the number of casualties taken was -- they were all civilians in there, as far as I was concerned. And there were equal number of women and children hurt in the use -- with the use of babies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It was a relatively small area, was it?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: It was, indeed, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about the ammunition factory to which you referred. The impression I have from your testimony is that Colonel Blaskic undertook to give notice in the event of his side deciding to blow up that factory; do you remember that part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He did give us warning of that, sir. He assured us he would give us two hours' notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: He said he would. If the factory blew up, would the establishment of BRITBAT be in jeopardy?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I don't doubt, sir, we would have suffered damage to a considerable degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Right. Now, are you in a position to tell us whether a similar undertaking to give notice was ever given on the HVO side in respect of any other explosions which they might have occasioned in the area within which you were located?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: No, they weren't, sir, and that includes the assault on Grbavica where rounds initially fell within the camp area before the mortars had zeroed in on their target. So no notice was given for that which was the closest, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last area of questioning has to do with this: HVO military personnel were located in groups in various places within Central Bosnia; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: From what you saw as a military man, would you be able to tell this Trial Chamber whether it was your impression that these various groups of eight HVO military personnel were acting in coordination one with another or they were acting completely on their own?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Our impression was that, as with all military units, they are given specific missions and tasks to undertake, but that is driven and directed by, for want of a better word, the policy makers. And that seemed to fit the picture in this case, as it does in most fields -- areas of conflict like this. There always seems to be a general policy operating behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say then that these various pockets of HVO military personnel were in communication, one with another, by some method or the other?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: Yes, they were, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have only one question to ask you, Captain, before we finish with this long testimony. It's one of the questions that my colleagues didn't ask but thought about this. Anto Valenta's politics or policy was very pre-eminent in respect of separation or the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan was to an advantage. My question is the following: When this policy, at the time that this type of policy is implemented, you who are a military man, when the military leader of the operative zone is chosen, is that person chosen as a result -- in respect of his own policies or the choices that he makes of that policy? Do you understand what I'm getting at?

utterances.speaker: LEE WHITWORTH
utterances.text: I do, indeed, sir, yes. And basing your question around the circumstances that I'm familiar with, we would say it's courses for courses. You would choose the person to undertake the task who you felt best equipped to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well, the Tribunal thanks you very sincerely. You have shown great patience. You have tried to answer honestly and in good faith, and objectively as it should be. For every witness, even if it is a witness for one of the two parties. We are grateful to you for that. You may now go back to your civilian activities, if I understood you correctly, and the registrar will have the witness escorted out of the courtroom. Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, what are you suggesting now? I have the feeling that you don't have any other witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we do not have any further witnesses for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, that will be advantageous to the interpreters and we are very thankful for their say because it hasn't been that easy for them. We are, therefore, glad we are ending early. Tomorrow we will resume at 10.00. Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.00 p.m. to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of July, 1998 at 10.00 a.m. 25
